en: Preface to the *Essential Pivot of the Ten Doors of Non-duality*:

This work explains the *Ten Doors of Non-duality*. However, since the multitude does not rely on the words but takes the meaning as primary, their realization of the meaning does not correspond to the words;
for the meaning shifts according to the mind. Thus, even the former masters were unable to remain silent, and so it is with us today. Regarding these ten doors—

Because it is composed for the purpose of contemplation, it is called "Contemplating the Mind. This work serves as the pivotal mechanism for the practice of the teachings; thus, it is titled with this essential term.
Preface written at the Mochan Hall on the Bingchen day of the eighth month in the Wuma year of the Shaoxing era.
The Essential Pivot of the Ten Gates of Non-Duality, Volume One.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Liaran of Huxi, East Corridor.
The Ten Gates of Non-Duality.
Someone asked: "Since these were recorded by later generations, how can one privately establish this title? The commentary states:

"In the *Tiantai Catalogue*, there are one fascicle each on the 'Six Identities' (*liuji*) and the 'Ten Suchnesses' (*shirushi*). These are now included in the *Great Collection* (*Dabu*) because they were circulated separately from the main body of the text;
hence they bear this designation. Now, we may take this as a precedent, applying it solely to the 'Ten Non-dualities' (*shibu'er*)."
There is no error in the four-character subtitle of the chapters; moreover, since it says, "Therefore, these ten gates are non-dual," this serves as the title.
Although the names [of the chapters] correspond to their respective contents, one should understand that they likely also intend a separate thematic application.

Furthermore, the primary intent of this text is to observe the teachings, while its secondary intent must be understood as observing the [practices]. This involves two aspects: first, regarding the texts from which the three divisions originate; second, regarding the single [text].

Regarding the principles transmitted within our family concerning the origins of the Three Sections (*sanbu*), the primary and secondary aspects correspond to one another, as stated in the *Yili* (Exemplary Rules):

"Whenever one intends to explain a meaning, one must first contemplate its categorical classification. For instance, although in the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra) the 'Contemplation of the Mind' (*guanxin*) is established beneath every doctrinal point, the fundamental intent of the text clarifies the Fivefold Profound Meaning (*wuchong xuanyi*), which excels all other teachings; thus, in this case, the teaching is primary and the contemplation is secondary."

Relying on phenomena to give rise to contemplation establishes the principle of "contemplating the mind. If one now applies the principles of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* using various teachings, the intent lies in employing the ten methods to perfect the wondrous contemplation;
thus, while the orthodox teaching is primary and the lineage of a single school is secondary, when it comes to the transmission, contemplation alone is considered correct.
Therefore, all three sections take contemplating the mind as their essential core. This is because Tiantai’s exposition of the sutras does not rely on mere enumeration.

Because the Dharma-treasure depends on others, one must establish the contemplation of the mind in accordance with the Buddha’s entrustment; if this contemplation is not established, there will be no means for those with the faculties of this degenerate age to enter the Way.
As the Buddha’s entrustment states: "If anyone believes what you have taught, they shall see me, and they shall also see you and the assembly of bhikṣus.
For this reason, Tiantai established his contemplations specifically based on these words of the entrustment. Thus it is said in the text: [End of Text]

Those below [the two superior types] may all cultivate contemplation to seek its essential meaning. Regarding the classification of their spiritual capacities (*gotra*) based on the two practices of faith and Dharma following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, we shall discuss them according to the predominant type.
If one does not practice the Dharma, there is no means by which one can enter; how much more so for one who practices the Dharma through reflection upon its meaning, which is still accessible.
One should understand that all phenomena are solely mind; thus, one should take the contemplation of the mind as the primary focus.

Precisely because it follows the text, the "Profound" (xuán) contemplates the collateral; yet because it exists within the contemplation of the Ten Profundities (shí miào), there is both presence and absence therein.
Now, following the essential intent, the "Profound" also contemplates the primary. Therefore, I have extracted the Ten Profundities to form these ten gates.

Since each gate is itself the wondrousness of the mind, there is nothing that is not contemplation. If one discusses the words of this contemplation in relation to the *Zhiguan*, they are contained herein.
To speak most concisely of the essential purport of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, the present text is quite comprehensive;

for the essential purport of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* does not transcend the three thousand [realms] as they are within a single thought-moment (*ekacitta*). Here, by pointing out that the three thousand are non-dual, one mind is revealed;

this mind is entirely wondrous, and this wondrousness does not exceed the ten [categories of] wondrousness. If one understands these ten wondrousnesses, then *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* can be known. Therefore, it is said: "One."

The period of transverse and longitudinal [expansion] does not go beyond a single thought-moment; the three thousand worlds are themselves the principle and realm of emptiness, provisionality, and the middle.

Even down to the benefitting of others, all is thus. Consequently, the ten stages of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight) constitute the present cause and effect of one’s own practice (*sva-pratipatti*), while the chapter on "arousing the teaching" constitutes the present capacity for transforming others (*parārtha*) and the objects so transformed.
If one does not first comprehend the essence of non-dual Dharma, yet wishes to expound these ten gates, it would likely be difficult.

Regarding those points that cannot yet be unified: first, the Three Truths constitute the non-dual essence, as it is said: "If not for the three thousand [realms] of emptiness, provisionality, and the mean";
second, emptiness and the mean constitute the non-dual essence, as it is said: "Because of the disappearance of purity and impurity, through emptiness and through the mean";
third, the Middle Way constitutes the non-dual essence, as it is said: "Neither provisional nor real"; fourth, the single nature constitutes [the non-dual essence].

Question: Regarding the statement that the non-dual essence (*advaya-tattva*) is fundamentally "one nature" or the "non-dual essence that transcends words and thought," how can there be four different ways of explaining its progression? Answer: That which transcends words and thought is precisely the single essence.
It is simply because the three truths are identical with the one emptiness, the one middle way, and the one non-duality; therefore, these four are [identical].
Thus, this very single dharma constitutes the non-dual essence; if one were to call it "one," it is nonetheless not "not-one.

Is this not precisely where the True Entry of Vimalakīrti lies? Although the name "Non-duality" originally derives from the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, the reason I have specifically adopted it as the title here is that, following the ten profundities (*myō*) of the Gate of Profound Traces, it is only in relation to the awakening to principle that the term "Opening" (*kai*) is applied.
Because it is manifest, it is said: "If one takes awakening to the principle as the standard, then the principle is neither provisional nor real;

not seeing a single dharma, the empty fist deceives small children. To speak of the provisional and the real is considered coarse; the principle is neither provisional nor real, and is therefore wondrous.
The *Shiqian* states: "All dharmas are extinguished and non-dual; yet, based again on awakening to the principle, the former [distinctions] are opened up."

The ten marvels—expedient means (*upāya*) and reality (*bhūta-artha*)—together constitute the single principle of the nature of mind (*citta-prakṛti*). That which is called "awakening to the principle" means opening up the expedient to reveal the real.
If one awakens to the true principle, that principle is neither expedient nor real; thus, expedient means and reality are non-dual. Therefore, the *Sūtra Commentary* (*Shu*) states:

"Now, by awakening to and entering into the non-duality of the three and the one, one knows that the Buddha’s teaching of the three and the one is without discrimination. The *Record* (*Ji*) states: "The following passage..."
In terms of principle, there is the provisional and the real; the non-duality of the provisional and the real constitutes the real.

This second explanation merely clarifies the principle of the previously mentioned Real Teaching (*śāsanadharma*). Since this principle is the non-duality of the provisional and the real, if it were not so, how could the text say:
"opening up the provisional to reveal the real, two yet non-two"? As for the term "gate" (*mukha*), it refers to this very non-duality.

The "gate" encompasses principle, teaching, and practice; that is, non-dual principle serves as the verbal expression (*vākya*), and non-dual principle serves as the contemplative practice (*bhāvanā*).

Both may be called "gates. Regarding *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, it is said: "Śamatha and vipaśyanā are practice, while the gate of non-arising (*anutpāda*) is the teaching. By relying on the teaching to cultivate practice, one universally attains the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At the stage of the cause, the thirty-two pure qualities of a bodhisattva, as described in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, are fully perfected. Each [of these]...
The *Introduction to the Gate of Non-duality* (*Faju wumen pin*) takes the gate of non-duality as its teaching. The *Profound Meaning* (*Xuanwen*) states:
"Regarding the practitioner, the true dharma of nirvāṇa is that sentient beings enter through various gates; the thirty-two bodhisattvas each enter the gate of non-dual dharmas.
This takes the gate of non-duality as its practice. The *Wondrous Verses* (*Miaoju*) states: "Even the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is dual."

Regarding the meaning: first, because its essential substance is empty and pervasive, it is called a "gate" (*mukha*). This is as in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, where one enters the "Gate of Non-duality.
Second, because it functions as a means for penetration, it is designated as a gate; the commentary states: "The single reality-principle receives its name from two [aspects];
because it is empty and pervasive, it causes others to take refuge therein. This takes the Gate of Non-duality as the principle. Now, following the specific discussion, by means of non-...
The second [section] concerns contemplating the entry into the principle of non-duality; because it is solely a contemplation that accords with the gate [of practice], it is called a "reiteration.

The ten gates are presented so that the contemplative practice may be recognized. As explained in the *Jingming wangji jieshu* (Commentary on the Extensive Record of Vimalakīrti), regarding the application of the ten types of fourfold propositions to explain the Gate of Non-duality, it says:
"As for the fourteenth proposition, although it is purely based on the gate of contemplation, despite the many gates, the intent lies in contemplation."
The Gate of Contemplation (*guanmen*) is explained last; however, as a gate that enables penetration, it possesses two meanings:
first, discussing penetration from the perspective of the subtle itself, whereby the contemplation of non-duality penetrates the principle of non-duality;
second, discussing penetration in contrast to the coarse, whereby one uses the contemplation of non-duality to penetrate duality, causing the dual to enter the gate of non-duality. That is to say:
Regarding all phenomena, one must realize and contemplate the principle of non-duality; this contemplation is not separate from the principle, for it is within the single mind.

By entering the mind through the mind, the mind is without dual characteristics. At that point, all dependencies are severed; in reality, there is neither a subject who enters nor an object to be entered.
Being free from all obstructions and attachments, flowing without hindrance and abiding nowhere—only then can it be called a "gate. Some say it is by means of the ten [stages].

Question: "Is it appropriate to say that the 'gates' (mēn) are that which enables penetration and the 'ten wonders' (shí miào) are that which is penetrated? Answer: "If one speaks of the gates as enabling and the wonders as being enabled, that may indeed be said.
However, we now establish ten gates to explain and penetrate the ten wonders; thus, we condense the ten wonders to form these ten gates.
One must simply not mistake the single character 'gate' for implying that they are established by following the perfect penetration of the ten wonders."

△ Commentary on the Text, in three parts: First, the general preface; second, the initial exposition of the Profound Text; third, the initial exposition of the Teaching. Within the first [exposition of the Teaching], there is the initial exposition:

"Now, this 'Trace Gate' (Jikimon) discusses its causes and effects as well as the self and the other, so that the various teaching-gates of a single lifetime may be harmonized and enter into the Subtle."
Xuanyun stated above that the four "wondrous names" constitute the perfect cause (*yuan-yin*), while the "secret treasury of the three dharmas" constitutes the perfect fruit (*yuan-guo*).

The *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary) states: "Regarding the four wondrous names as the cause: if 'position-wonder' (*wei-miao*) is established as being real, it pervades both cause and fruit; however, in contrast to the three dharmas, it is here spoken of from the perspective of the cause.
Furthermore, if explained according to its specific distinction, the loftiness and profundity of this particular stage constitutes its own independent meaning."

Thus, the five wondrous existences (pañca-mithyā-sat) are both horizontal and vertical. Horizontally, they pertain to their respective positions where both height and depth encompass both cause and fruit.

Vertically, they are discussed in terms of delusion and awakening, being restricted to the distinction between cause and fruit. Within the vertical classification, the first three are exclusively causes, while the latter one is exclusively the stage of the fruit.
Regarding the wondrous [existence], it generally encompasses both cause and fruit; however, when specifically restricted to the cause, there is furthermore...

Regarding "pervasive" and "limited": if pervasive, it encompasses both the stage of contemplative practice (*guanxing*) and the stage of semblance (*xiangsi*). The *Zhuan* (Commentary) states: "As for the stages reached by practice, there are various positions.

If one takes what is reached by practice as the position itself, then not only are the positions pervasive across the stages of contemplative practice, but the practice itself is also pervasive across the stage of semblance.

However, if one defines the position based on what is reached by practice, then practice is limited to the stage of contemplative practice, and the position is limited to the stage of semblance. This is because [the position] is determined by what is reached through practice.
Regarding the stages, there are various positions; because they are situated after the practice-positions (*gyō-i*), they are restricted to the ten stages of faith (*jūshin*).

Regarding the ancient commentaries on the two views of self and other, the correct principle (*sei-gi*) holds that the first five wondrous functions are "self" and the latter five wondrous functions are "other.

The *Shiyō-monshin* and *En-tsū* agree with this, maintaining that the latter five wondrous functions, being capable of transformation, constitute "self," while that which is transformed constitutes "other. This [present] explanation is the correct one.

In the former case, the meaning captures the essence of the Dharma while the text loses its source; in the latter, the essential point captures the source of the text while the essence of the Dharma is lost. Why is this so?

If one relies on the essence of the Dharma itself, it is identical to emptiness, just as in the previous discussion of one’s own practice (*svayam-caryā*). As the eighth fascicle of the *Shi* (Notes) states:

"As explained in the Ten Profound Subtleties (*daśa-sūkṣmatā*), there is one's own practice from cause to fruit, as well as the practice for transforming others. Therefore, we know that what is said here [refers to this].
Regarding the discussion of cause and effect as well as self and others: the word "self" refers to one's own practice.

As for the text that follows, it appears later in the five treatises; therein, the responsive resonance (*saṃgēn*) of the transformer and the transformed constitutes the essence (the "self"), while benefiting others is the "other.
Therefore, it says, "as well as self and others," and we shall see this when reaching the section on self and others; what is discussed now pertains to a single lifetime.

The "teaching gates" refer to the five periods and four teachings. Regarding the causes and effects of self and others discussed in the Trace Gate (Jikimon), it is intended to lead one to understand that the coarseness of the three teachings across the four periods merges into the subtlety of the Perfect Teaching of the Lotus Sūtra. △ Second, the Proof.

Therefore, all explanations of various meanings are based upon the four teachings and the five flavors, with the intention that the teachings be opened up so that all may enter the *tīrthaṅkara* (the ultimate essence).
Throughout the *Xuánwén*, all explanations regarding the meanings of cause and effect, self and other, and so forth, are likewise based upon the four teachings and the five flavors.
Regarding "tasting," the intention is to open up the coarseness of the four flavors and three teachings so that one may enter the subtlety of the *paramārtha* (ghee) of the Perfect Teaching;

thus, what was said previously—that it enables the various gates of the One Lifetime’s teachings to be harmonized and enter the subtle—is not empty talk. Second, the exposition of contemplation, which has two parts:
first, the exposition of this school’s taking contemplation as the primary focus.
Contemplating the mind is the pivotal mechanism of both teaching and practice.

The *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) states that regarding cause and effect, self and others, and so forth, one must rely on contemplating the mind to enter the Way; if it were not for contemplating the mind, there would be no gateway to entering the Way.
Is this not because contemplating the mind is the essential core of teaching and practice? Thus, we know that in the present text, contemplation is established as the primary principle.
The *Zhijyao* (Essentials of the Pointing) states: "All teachings and practices take the contemplation of the mind as their essential;

all arise from the contemplation of the mind. Because the mind contemplated is empty, all things are empty. These four points take the attainment of the path and its virtues through the contemplation of the mind as essential.
The *Wenxin* (Text of the Mind) states: "The ultimate destination of the teachings and the source of practice lie in the contemplation of the mind. The subsequent text says: "If one understands..."

In a single thought-moment, the Dharma of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time—both their fundamental and manifested aspects—is not remote; this is the essential point of the Teaching.

Furthermore, since the causes within the minds of sentient beings already possess the three tracks (*trividha-yāna*), when these causes result in fruition, they are called the three nirvāṇas; this is the essential point of Practice.
This is the "Essential Guide to the Core Meaning" (*Wénxīn chéngyòng zhǐyào zhèngyì*) which states: "If the Teaching lacks the contemplation of the mind, it becomes nothing more than empty words."

The practice of cultivation arises from nowhere else than the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*). Regarding both the teaching and its application, this is like the pivot of a door or the trigger of a crossbow;
it is said to be the essential point. Yuan Tong asked: "When the sages established the teachings, they were called 'teachings' (*jiao*);
why then do you take the contemplation of the mind as the pivot and trigger? He replied: "The sages established the teachings primarily to cause one to contemplate the mind. If not..."
Contemplating the mind is called "valuing another’s treasure. He asked again: "Regarding 'practice is precisely contemplating the mind,' how does one contemplate the mind as the pivot of practice?
The answer was: "Exquisite practice must take the contemplation of the mind as its essential. If one does not contemplate the mind, it is not the fundamental pivot of practice.

Therefore, in *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, one discards the fathom for the cubit, and discards the cubit for the inch; setting aside the four aggregates such as form, one contemplates only the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*)."

The "contemplation of the mind" (*guanxin*) is like cauterizing a disease to find its precise point or felling a tree by finding its root; is it not the case that contemplating the mind is precisely the pivotal essential of wondrous practice? This is the correct principle upheld and employed by the various masters of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*).

While none of them [exclusively] rely on the transmitted tenets of a single school, today, for entering the Path, contemplation is regarded as the primary requirement. Furthermore, [The text continues: ...it is said that the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is like the ocean; the various vehicles are like the rivers flowing into it. Although the teachings differ according to the capacities of those to be converted, they all ultimately converge upon the One Vehicle. Therefore, one should know that the contemplation of the mind is the gateway through which all Buddhas enter the Path. It is the supreme method for severing the bonds of affliction and the most direct means for attaining the fruit of Buddhahood. Thus, those who wish to cultivate the Way must first establish this contemplation as their fundamental practice. If one does not contemplate the mind, one will be unable to perceive the true nature of reality. Without perceiving the true nature, one cannot escape birth and death. Therefore, the contemplation of the mind is the most urgent matter for those seeking liberation. It is the very lifeblood of the Mahāyāna. To neglect it is to abandon the core of the Buddha's intent. To embrace it is to hold fast to the ultimate truth. May all practitioners take this to heart and apply themselves with diligence. Thus ends this brief exposition. May it serve as a guide for future seekers. May all beings attain enlightenment. *Namo Amitābha*. *Namo Mañjuśrī*. *Namo Avalokiteśvara*. *Namo Mahāsthāmaprāpta*. *Namo Śākyamuni*. *Namo Sarvabuddhabodhisattvas*. May the merit of this writing be dedicated to all sentient beings, that they may quickly realize the unconditioned, wondrous, and perfect enlightenment. *Svāhā*. (Note: The final portion of the provided text fragment contains standard concluding invocations and dedications typical of Chinese Buddhist liturgical and exegetical works.)

Although the *Yuan-tong* (Complete Penetration) states that the Sage’s teaching is intended to cause one to contemplate the mind (*guanxin*), it subsequently says, "It is like cauterizing a disease at its correct point.

Is this not to say that contemplating the mind alone is the essential practice? Nevertheless, the *Yuan-tong* errs in two respects: first, it fails to recognize that contemplating all three divisions [of the body] is the correct method;
second, since it does not permit the "Ten Gates of Non-duality" (*Shier Buermen*) as a secondary teaching, it fails to acknowledge its own limitations.

If you observe that [the text] speaks of the "correct" (zheng) and yet says, "If there were no contemplation (guan), it would be called teaching and would merely be counting another's treasures," then I now ask:
can it not be said that the "wondrous teaching" (miaojiao) is precisely the pivot of contemplation of the mind?

If it cannot be so, is it not the case that the teaching is ancillary (bang) to the correct contemplation? △ Second, showing the categories [of texts] where contemplation is ancillary. Part one: showing contemplation.
Section Two: General Demonstration of the First [Part], Subsection One: Comparing the Extensiveness and Brevity of Names Relative to Other Schools.
This shall, for now, be briefly indicated as it is situated within various expositions.

When compared with the extensiveness of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, the *Xuánwén* (Profound Meaning) is considered brief; this brief indication is thus situated within the various sections of the *Xuánwén*.

The *Miaohou shuoqian* (Notes on the Sublime Explanations) states: "If one examines the ten [sections] on the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*), they are all appended to the end of the various texts.

Furthermore, the reason the *Xuanyu wen* (Profound Meaning) provides only a brief indication of the contemplation of the mind is that the meaning of contemplating the mind is entrusted to the various expositions in the *Zhi guan* (Cessation and Contemplation), the *Si nian chu* (Four Mindfulnesses), and the *Xiao zhiguan* (Shorter Cessation and Contemplation). △ Second, an analysis of what is retained and what is omitted within the present section.
Whether [the ten sections] are present or omitted is not the primary intention of this division.

This is because, according to the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text), these are considered ancillary to the "Contemplation of the Mind" (*guānxīn*) section; thus, they may be present or omitted. The *Qiān* (Annotations) states:

"The ten sections for both the Fundamental and the Traces are fully listed in the text; however, the ten sections for the Contemplation of the Mind are either present or omitted and do not constitute separate chapters."
△ Second, the specific demonstration.

Therefore, even if there are provisional establishments (*prajñapti*) that rely on phenomena or attach to dharmas, they merely enumerate the names of the ten contemplations. While the previous section provided a general indication of what exists and what has ceased, this section provides a specific demonstration of what remains;

even if something does remain, its provisional establishment— *Note: The original text appears to be a commentary on a Buddhist scholastic work (likely concerning the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* or related Tathāgatagarbha thought), discussing the status of various doctrinal categories.*

Regarding the categories of "relying on phenomena" (*shōji*) and "attaching to the Dharma" (*fuhō*), or "following practice" (*jūgyō*): since these three types are not the primary [method], their names alone are listed.
Furthermore, as for listing the names, they are distinguished by being categorized under "following practice. Question: Regarding the "Ten Contemplations," these are the Ten Vehicles (*jūjō*).

If one relies on phenomena or attaches to the Dharma, one likewise cultivates the Ten Contemplations; why then is this specifically designated here as "following practice"? Answer: As for the Ten Vehicles—

The "general essence" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) refers to the three types of contemplative methods; the "specific characteristics" (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) refer to the three types of contemplative methods as they rely on phenomena and attach to the Dharma for the sake of practitioners.
Practicing the ten vehicles by relying on the phenomena that serve as the basis for representation is called "contemplation based on phenomena" (*tòshì guān*);

practicing the ten vehicles by relying on the characteristics of the Dharma gates is called "contemplation attached to the Dharma" (*fùfǎ guān*). Apart from these two, [there is] that which relies on...
Regarding the statement that "the ten vehicles are cultivated across the myriad realms," this is called the Contemplation of Following Practice (*cong xing guan*).

Zhiyi’s text takes the general essence of the ten vehicles as the specific name for this contemplation; thus, the Contemplation of Following Practice is said to be "the ten vehicles, as explained in the separate chapter. II.
Clarifying the Correctness of the Teaching (Three parts): A. First, analyzing the character *miao* (wondrous).

Regarding the principles, objects, wisdom, practices, stages, and dharmas clarified herein—both the means of transformation and those to be transformed—the intent lies in the expressive terminology (*vyañjana*), and within that expression, all is wondrous.
The "expressive terminology" refers to the name *Saddharma* (Wondrous Dharma) of this present sutra;

within this expression, the seven categories of truths from the beginning and the ten rounds of benefit at the end each encompass their respective time and teaching through their revelation, and thus they all receive the name "Wondrous. △ Second, the analysis of the ten [wondrous aspects].
The title:
In order to discern and explain the beginning and end, as well as the self and others within [the Buddha’s teaching], the tenfold mysteries are fully expounded.

Xuanyan states: "Although the dharmas are immeasurable, the meaning of these ten principles is perfectly complete; 'perfect' means being universally and completely endowed with the correct principle. Zhengyi states: "[This refers to] one's own practice..."

Taking the "sublimity of the object" as the beginning and the "three dharmas" as the end constitutes the transformation of others; taking "responsive resonance" as the beginning and "benefiting others" as the end constitutes the benefit of others.

Now, to provide proof for this, Xuán says: "The first five [categories] concern one's own practice, being complete in cause and effect; the latter five concern the ability to transform others, being complete in both the agent and the object.
Thus, the beginning and end of both self and others are all brought to ultimate fulfillment. The *Shìjiǎn* states: "This concludes the section on one's own [practice]."
The practices for transforming others each have their beginning and end; since it is stated that they "each" possess these, this can serve as proof.

Furthermore, at the beginning, there are five because they concern the causes and effects of one's own practice (*sva-pratipatti*); at the end, there are likewise five because they concern the agent and object of transforming others (*para-parāvṛtti*).
This is because the present text first sets forth the beginning and end, which differs from the *Xuánwén*. △ Third, concluding with the *Fǎhuá*.
The great purport of the single transformation for transcending the world has been thoroughly investigated and exhaustively set forth, leaving nothing out.

Since the ten subtleties have been expounded, the matters of the single transformation are fully exhausted; since the single transformation is fully exhausted, the purport of transcending the world is completely realized.
If it were not for the subtle exposition of the *Lotus Sūtra*, how could the meaning of this transformation ever be fully understood? △ Second, the account of the present.
By composing the first four [chapters], he establishes the contemplation based on the teachings;

therefore, one must not fail to understand the general outline of the Ten Profound Subtleties (*daśa-sūkṣmatā*). Thus, he summarizes the Ten Profound Subtleties as the fundamental framework for the method of contemplation.

When correctly clarifying the teachings, the Ten Profound Subtleties can be fully exhausted; however, if one wishes to enter the Path, it is necessary to comprehend this general outline of the Ten Profound Subtleties.

The teachings are like the meshes of a net, while the essentials for contemplating the mind (*citta*) are like its main cord. In the preceding text, contemplating the mind was treated as the pivotal mechanism;
in the present text, contemplating phenomena (*dharma*) is treated as the essential body of the main cord. Is it not the case that contemplating the mind is the foundation for entering the Way?

This main cord consists precisely of the Ten Profound Subtleties (*daśa-prakarṣa*). When this main cord exists, the non-duality of form and mind constitutes the subtlety of the object (*viṣaya-prakarṣa*). Thus, the main cord is...
Reaching the stage of receiving moisture and non-duality constitutes the two great outlines for benefiting the retinue.

Regarding the two as phenomena (*vastu*), as the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Practice) states: "The three truths have no form and are all invisible;

yet, by means of conventional dharmas (*prajñapti-dharma*), one may rely upon phenomena to discern them, even to the point of provisionally establishing the name 'Middle,' provisionally establishing the designation 'Emptiness,' and provisionally establishing the appellation 'Conventional.

To point to the three as being the conventional is precisely for the conventional to be the phenomenon. Furthermore, it clearly states: "One may rely upon phenomena to discern them. Is this not indeed illumination?
Question: Regarding the "three as phenomena" (*shi*), what is the meaning of "phenomena" (*shi*) in relation to the three truths (*sandi*), which are the natural, inherent virtues?

Answer: The meanings of the three truths in terms of principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*) do not follow a single path. If one considers them from the perspective of their transcendent virtues, the three truths constitute principle and the three delusions constitute phenomena;

thus, they can be called the natural, inherent virtues. However, if one considers them from the perspective of non-extinction and illumination (*wangzhao*), then the single nature constitutes principle.

The third [category] is named "phenomena" (*vastu*); therefore, it can be said that provisional dharmas may rely upon phenomena for their discernment, and while one may grasp at faults or virtues, the illumination [of reality] cannot be lost.

If one were to claim this is not so—citing that the Great Master [Zhiyi] sometimes takes the Middle Way as principle (*li*) and the True and Conventional as phenomena, or that the True and the Middle are principle while the Conventional Truth is phenomena—how could Jingxi [Zhanran] have stated that all three are nature-virtues (*xingde*)?

Question: Since the three [aspects of] illumination correspond to the three [realms of] phenomena, then phenomena are identical to emotion. Should the triad of emptiness, provisional existence, and the middle not also belong to emotion? Answer:

The substance of the three delusions and the three paths is indeed emotion—like raw jade or impurity. The triad of emptiness, provisional existence, and the middle is like the whetstone and the hammer.

Because one treats the three delusions by means of these, one establishes three provisional names upon the single nature. Since these names are obtained through emotion, [the categories of] emptiness and provisional existence [are so designated].

The Middle is entangled by emotional afflictions (*kleśa*), and thus it receives a designation based on its phenomenal activity; however, Emptiness, Provisionality, and the Middle themselves are not emotional afflictions.

Above, the three names were established based on the capacity to possess the single nature in order to explain it. If we consider what is possessed—the two extremes of Emptiness and Provisionality—their substance is ignorance, and they are likewise subsumed under emotional afflictions.
Furthermore, the nature is fundamentally nameless; it is only because of conditions that it is provisionally attached to worldly designations.
As the Great Master (Zhiyi) established: "The Buddha fundamentally has no body, no lifespan, and no measure;

yet, in accordance with worldly convention, one speaks of three bodies, three lifespans, and three measures. Since these three names are established in conformity with the world, is the world not a reality?
Now, this case is likewise. Furthermore, Jingxi (Zhanran) said: "The names and titles of the Tathāgata differ by a hundred thousand; [this is] like the *Prajñāpāramitā*..."
A single dharma is spoken of by various names; liberation is likewise characterized by many appellations. These are called "conformity with sentiment. Now, this case is treated by analogy. Question:
May the three illuminations be taken as the True Principle? May the three virtues be taken as arising from sentiment? Answer:

One who studies Buddhism extensively must thoroughly understand the essence of dharmas (*dharmatā*). If the essence of dharmas is not clearly understood, one will produce interpretations merely following the literal words.

If one generates understanding merely by following the literal words, the mind and its principles will become confused. One should know that the three—truth (*satya*), convention (*saṃvṛti*), and the middle (*madhyama*)—are but a single dharma-substance;

they are distinguished according to their respective meanings. Thus, while faults may arise, virtues are lost, and there are differences such as illumination and so forth. If these three are taken from the perspective of nature (*svabhāva*), then because they are identical to that nature, the three constitute principle (*li*).
If these three are taken from the perspective of phenomena (*vastu*), then because the three are established in accordance with phenomena, the three constitute phenomena (*shi*). For example:

If one asks whether the three [aspects] of illumination are not precisely the nature itself, the answer is yes. Furthermore, if one asks whether the three [aspects] of virtue are not established based on phenomena, the answer is yes.

However, because they serve to distinguish meanings and each has its own basis, when referring to "non-existence" (the aspect of cessation), we establish the three based on the side of being attached to phenomena;

this is because the names belong to the attributes. When referring to "transgressions" or "virtues," we establish the three based on the side of identity with the nature; this is because they belong to the essence. If, regarding non-existence...
When illumination grasps [the three] by taking their very nature as the three bodies (trikāya), they are therefore called the "Three Truths.
If, regarding the virtues, one grasps them by attaching them to phenomena as the three names, they are therefore called the "three phenomenal matters" (vastu). Question:
While it may be said that the three names are established based on phenomena, what is the basis for the essence (svabhāva) of the [Buddha] below? What is its inherent nature?

Furthermore, regarding the three capacities that express phenomena, one may say these are "three matters" (three phenomena). How then are the three principles expressed by them? What are these matters? Answer:
Ultimately, when scrutinizing the reality, are there three entities? Are there three principles? If you say there are, why did the Patriarch say:
"Although there are three names, there are no three entities"? And since he said, "Although it is a single entity, three names are established," if this is granted...
Because these three names refer to phenomena, one knows that the three are themselves the phenomena.

Since it is said that the substance underlying a name and the principle (li) expressed by that name are designated as "principle" (li), and since both substance and principle are thus established, one can be certain that the single nature is indeed the principle.
Those who wish to clarify the mind should reflect upon this carefully; if you do not accept this, you may be questioned further now.
Now, as for the Three Truths, since they are the natural, inherent virtue, being "natural" means they are primordially present.

I have not yet examined whether this primordially present reality possesses three names or three essences. If one says that the primordially present has three names, why does the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) state:

"The principle is originally nameless; it is only through force that designations are established"? If one says that the primordially present has three essences, [it contradicts the teaching of] cessation...
The *Guān* says: "Although there are three names, there are no three entities. Please explain this for me. Question:

If the essence (*tī*) of the Three Truths were one, why does the *Fǔxíng* say that "the essence of the truths is eternally three"? Answer: This is explained by discerning the essence according to the names.
If one discusses the essence from the perspective of its actual reality (*kèshí*), it is said that although there are three names, there are no [three distinct] entities.
Question: Regarding the attachment of the three bodies to phenomena—part three—is this circular fusion (*yuanrong*) or sequential separation (*gelili*)?
Answer: Because the three are identical to the essence (*ti*), the three belong to circular fusion; because the three are attached to phenomena (*shi*), the three belong to differentiation.
However, this differentiation is the differentiation of equality, and the circular fusion is the separation of the undivided. Why? Because from the single essence, the three are established.

Question: Why is there a sequential distinction within the Perfect and Sudden Teaching? Answer: The *Myōgen* (The Profound Meaning) clarifies that regarding the dharma-gates and their retinues in the Perfect Teaching, it states:
"The single truth or three truths according to [sentient beings'] dispositions are provisional. It further states: "The one truth or three truths for the sake of transforming others are provisional.

The *Myōku* (The Profound Words) explains the expedients of the Perfect Teaching by stating: "The provisional possesses distinctions," and it also explains the provisional within the Perfect Teaching.

Regarding the statement that all dharmas are established as having different grades and distinctions: since the three truths of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) are already designated as "provisional" (quan), and since they are both "Perfect" and "provisional," yet remain distinct, one may also say that the three truths of the Perfect Teaching constitute differentiation.

Furthermore, in his *Commentary on the Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Zhanran clearly explains that the single truth is identical to the three truths, such that there is no difference between non-differentiation and differentiation.
It is for this reason that it is now called the "differentiation of equality. Furthermore, differentiation is precisely what is meant by "separation" (*gelilè*).

Is it not, therefore, termed the "separation of perfect fusion" (*yuanrong*)? Thus, in the *Fuxing Zhuan* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), while distinguishing between the three truths and four truths of the Perfect Teaching, the text states:
"Question: The three and four [truths] of the previous [teachings] may be considered horizontal or vertical, and even fused; but how can the three and four of the Perfect [Teaching] be so?"

The horizontal and vertical responses are indeed as you have asked. Now, regarding what is called "horizontal and vertical": within the context of the Three Truths, for instance, taking one truth and opening it into two or three is termed "vertical.
Taking those two or three as a provisional means (*upāya*)—wherein the means is viewed in relation to the reality—is also termed "vertical.
When the provisional is opened to reveal the reality, there is no longer any duality or plurality; what then could be discussed as "vertical"? Since this does not apply to the single reality...
If one divides [the truths] into three, what prevents these three from being neither horizontal nor vertical, yet being called "vertical"?

The same applies to the four truths. According to the provisional teachings (*upāya-deśanā*), they may be described as horizontal; however, the four unconditioned truths (*anabhisaṃskāra-catur-āryasatya*) are fundamentally mutually identical.
With whom could one discuss horizontality? Furthermore, if one divides that which is undivided into the four truths, what prevents them from not being horizontal?

That which is not vertical is called horizontal, as in the six stages of position; that which is neither horizontal nor vertical is called vertical; and since the various *pāramitās* are neither horizontal nor vertical yet are called horizontal, we know that horizontal and vertical, high and broad, are non-dual. Question: What was previously discussed was "specific" (*bhedaka*); why then speak of the "general" (*sāmānya*)? Answer: When analyzed according to the essential nature of phenomena, they are "specific" only in terms of their particular manifestations. As for the "general," it refers to the fact that all phenomena share the same essence. Furthermore, while the specific refers to the distinctness of individual entities, the general refers to the fact that these entities are identical in their fundamental nature. Thus, although they appear as distinct, they are ultimately one. This is why the general is spoken of. Furthermore, the specific refers to the differentiation of the various gates of practice, whereas the general refers to the fact that all such gates ultimately converge in a single principle. Therefore, the specific and the general are non-dual. This is why the general is spoken of. Furthermore, the specific refers to the distinctions among the various teachings and practices, while the general refers to the fact that all teachings and practices are subsumed within the single Dharma-realm. Therefore, the specific and the general are non-dual. This is why the general is spoken of. Furthermore, the specific refers to the differences in the capacities and inclinations of sentient beings, while the general refers to the fact that all capacities and inclinations are ultimately of one taste. Therefore, the specific and the general are non-dual. This is why the general is spoken of. Furthermore, the specific refers to the distinctions in the various methods of cultivation, while the general refers to the fact that all methods of cultivation are unified in the realization of the true nature. Therefore, the specific and the general are non-dual. This is why the general is spoken of. Furthermore, the specific refers to the diversity of the phenomena of birth and death, while the general refers to the fact that all phenomena of birth and death are fundamentally quiescent and identical to Nirvana. Therefore, the specific and the general are non-dual. This is why the general is spoken of. Furthermore, the specific refers to the differences in the various stages of the path, while the general refers to the fact that all stages of the path are ultimately the same Buddha-ground. Therefore, the specific and the general are non-dual. This is why the general is spoken of. Therefore, the specific and the general are non-dual. This is why the general is spoken of. Furthermore, the specific refers to the differences in the various vehicles, while the general refers to the fact that all vehicles are ultimately the One Vehicle. Therefore, the specific and the general are non-dual. This is why the general is spoken of. Furthermore, the specific refers to the distinctions in the various forms of merit and virtue, while the general refers to the fact that all merit and virtue are ultimately subsumed within the single thought-moment of the Bodhi-mind. Therefore, the specific and the general are non-dual. This is why the general is spoken of. Therefore, the specific and the general are non-dual. This is why the general is spoken of. Furthermore, the specific refers to the distinctions in the various aspects of the teachings, while the general refers to the fact that all teachings are ultimately the same Great Vehicle. Therefore, the specific and the general are non-dual. This is why the general is spoken of. Therefore, the specific and the general are non-dual. This is why the general is spoken of. Furthermore, the specific refers to the distinctions in the various types of obstacles, while the general refers to the fact that all obstacles are ultimately the same enlightenment. Therefore, the specific and the general are non-dual. This is why the general is spoken of. Furthermore, the specific refers to the differences in the various types of wisdom, while the general refers to the fact that all wisdom is ultimately the same mirror-like wisdom. Therefore, the specific and the general are non-dual. This is why the general is spoken of. Furthermore, the specific refers to the distinctions in the various types of vows, while the general refers to the fact that all vows are ultimately the same vow for the benefit of others. Therefore, the specific and the general are non-dual. This is why the general is spoken of. Furthermore, the specific refers to the differences in the various types of practices, while the general refers to the fact that all practices are ultimately the same practice of the Six Perfections. Therefore, the specific and the general are non-dual. This is why the general is spoken of. Furthermore, the specific refers to the distinctions in the various types of fruits, while the general refers to the fact that all fruits are ultimately the same fruit of Buddhahood. Therefore, the specific and the general are non-dual. This is why the general is spoken of. Therefore, the specific and the general are non-dual. This is why the general is spoken of. Furthermore, the specific refers to the differences in the various types of skillful means, while the general refers to the fact that all skillful means are ultimately the same great skillful means.
