If there were no internal, there would be no external; if there were no external, there would be no internal. Therefore, the internal and external are non

This gate takes the three truths and one reality as the essence of non-duality; therefore, both the internal and external objects are said to be "immediately empty, provisional, and middle," and further described as being "only the single reality-nature.
Here, "internal and external" refers—according to the explanation provided below—to nothing other than the three dharmas:
form and mind. Question: In the previous gate on form and mind, the three dharmas of form and mind were also discussed; why is this so?

This is considered a different answer: form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) constitute the universal essence of these three dharmas, while the three dharmas are the specific characteristics of form and mind.
Previously, form and mind were distinguished by means of the three dharmas, hence it was said that "form and mind are non-dual.

Now, the three dharmas are distinguished by means of form and mind, hence it is said that "internal and external are non-dual. Failing to perceive this meaning, some merely prattle on in vain. △ Second, the explanation.
Furthermore, the first three [sections] provide a general outline.
Whatever objects are observed do not transcend the internal or the external.
Yuan Tong says: "Although the observing contemplation itself has no distinction, the objects observed must be distinguished as internal or external."

This is because, according to the principle of the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), principle is identical to phenomena; therefore, there are distinctions among the ten objects such as the five aggregates (*skandhas*).
It cannot be argued that because phenomena are identical to principle, every single object is inconceivable. Furthermore, it says:

"If one were to follow ordinary sentiment and differentiate them thus, [it would be so]; now we say that since these two—internal and external—are already within the realm of the conceivable, they accord with [ordinary sentiment].
Regarding the analysis of the nature of phenomena: why is it that while matter and mind are themselves inconceivable, they instead conform to the Dharma-gate of the three thousandfold world?

If one points to the analysis of matter and mind as being already perfect and wondrous—the three thousandfold world—why then distinguish between internal and external, which would instead be a conceivable, deluded state? If you say this is because they conform to the objects of contemplation, then consider matter itself...

Is it not the case that the mind is not the object of contemplation? If you claim that the aforementioned matter and mind constitute a "wondrous realm," then since it is a wondrous realm, it ought to be non-dual; how can both matter and mind be dual while still being a wondrous realm?
Furthermore, if you say that as soon as one speaks of a "wondrous realm" matter and mind are non-dual, for what reason do you then separately divide matter and mind into three?
Regarding the phrase "thousand wondrous realms" and "internal and external," these encompass the three dharmas as well as form and mind.
Why? Since both sentient beings and Buddhas are taken as "external," one's own self is taken as "internal" (this applies to the three dharmas).
Since one's own mind is taken as "internal," one's own form is taken as "external" (this applies to form and mind). If distinguished according to the literal text, it is by means of the self...
One’s own mind and dharmas constitute the internal; the Buddha’s reliance and manifestation (the environment and the body), as well as form and mind, constitute the external.
Furthermore, they are neither the three dharmas nor merely form and mind. This is because the present text sets aside and does not discuss the colors of one’s own reliance and manifestation;

rather, it intends to comprehensively encompass them through the meaning of the three dharmas, thereby allowing the colors of one’s own reliance and manifestation to include both the internal and the external.
If discussed in terms of principle (*li*), they belong to the internal; if discussed in terms of form and mind (*rūpa-citta*), they belong to the external.
If one compares the text to clarify this, then the current passage should be understood as dividing the three dharmas into internal and external. Why? According to the subsequent text, it asks:
"Who says there are internal and external, form and mind, self and other? Now, if internal form and mind constitute the self, and external form and mind constitute the other, is this not so?

The three dharmas are divided into internal and external. As for why the preceding text did not discuss one's own physical form (*rūpa-dharma*), it was because one observes one's own mind from the perspective of what is proximate and essential;
thus, it merely demonstrated mindfulness and non-mindfulness within oneself, focusing solely on the internal three thousand [realms].
In fact, even one's own physical form, when viewed in relation to sentient beings and Buddhas, is also internal; therefore, it is said that both internal and external form and mind belong to oneself.
His contemplation of Guanyin is essentially the same as the present text. That [text] states that the "object" is further divided into two:

namely, self and other. "Other" refers to sentient beings and Buddhas; "self" refers to that which is inherent within the mind. Furthermore, regarding one's own person, it does not speak of form, which is likewise consistent with the *smṛtyupasthāna* (foundations of mindfulness).
When externally contemplating the ten dharma-realms, one immediately perceives the ten realms of birth and Buddhahood within the internal mind.

Therefore, it is said that seeing one's own mind externally is called "internal. Regarding this "self," it is also not spoken of in terms of form (*rūpa*). Furthermore, in the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), it says:
"Even if one knows that the internal mind possesses the three thousand dharmas, if one does not know that my mind pervades those three thousand [dharmas]," and so on, concluding:
"Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—how could it be that one's own mind is 'internal' while the Buddhas born from sentient beings are 'external'?"
Regarding oneself as well, one does not speak of "form. △ Second, the formal explanation, which has two parts; first, the explanation of the external, which further has two parts.
First, showing the object and the contemplation:
"External" refers to the environment and its inhabitants, as well as form and mind, which are themselves emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.

The other-lives and other-Buddhas each possess their own environment and inhabitants, as well as form and mind; these belong to the external. However, when this realm has not yet been realized, it belongs to delusion;
once it is realized, it is the True. Why is this? Because it is precisely the Three Truths. △ Second, showing the extinction and illumination.
Part one: showing the two. First, showing extinction.

Because the wondrous nature of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle is such that the substance of form and mind is transcended, there is only the single true nature, devoid of emptiness, the provisional, or the middle.

Regarding the substance of one’s own mind: if one distinguishes its substance according to names, one is distinguishing its substance according to names; if one discusses its substance by grasping the reality, one is discussing its substance.

If one distinguishes its substance according to names, it is the differentiated substance signified by the names "sentient beings and Buddhas," "the dependent and the primary," and "form and mind. As for these differences...
There are sentient beings, there are Buddhas, there is the dependent and the primary, and there are form and mind; each has its own distinct substance.

However, if one investigates the reality of their substance, then sentient beings and Buddhas, as well as the dependent and the primary, form and mind, all take the same True Nature as their substance, and in truth there is no difference between them.
What is now said regarding "the substance of form and mind being severed" is merely a discernment of substance according to names.
If the essence could be severed, then in a true discussion of essence, how could that essence be severed? The Patriarch said: "It is not that the essence of the mind is empty and non-existent.

Rather, it is because the essence of the distinctions between the Buddha and sentient beings, and between the primary and secondary realms, is severed through the wondrous efficacy of the three contemplations. Why is this?

Because one realizes that the form and mind of the Buddha and sentient beings, as well as the primary and secondary realms, are themselves the perfect fusion of emptiness, provisional existence, and the Middle Way.
Because it is one, it is able to sever the deluded substance of differentiation; once the deluded substance is severed, the true nature is revealed.
Thus it is said that there is only the single true nature, which is devoid of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. Regarding the phrase "devoid of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle":

first, the three contemplations are fundamentally intended to illuminate the deluded objects so that the objects become identical with the truth; now that the objects have already become true, what further use would there be for the contemplations? Second, [the text continues...]
By means of contemplation one contemplates the object; within that object there is both the real and the false. Now, regarding the discussion of the true object of contemplation:
if the true object is taken as the three truths, then the contemplating observation is emptiness, provisional existence, and the middle;

if the true object is taken as the single reality, then the contemplating observation is neither emptiness, nor provisional existence, nor the middle. Therefore, the contemplating observation is solely the observation of single reality, which arises from the truth.

Regarding the objects [of cognition], there is "extinction" (wang) and there is "illumination" (zhao). Extinction means that within the True, the Conventional, and the Middle, there is only a single nature.

Illumination means that within the True, the Conventional, and the Middle, there are three truths. Now, since the true object is thus characterized by the extinction of the three and the presence of only the one real nature, the observing subject likewise extinguishes the three and is without emptiness, the provisional, or the middle. △ Second, showing illumination.
Form and mind appear vividly, suddenly opening up to be identical with true purity.
Previously, it was shown that because form and mind have perished, their substance is severed and there is only the single true nature;

now it is shown that because form and mind are illuminated, they appear vividly, suddenly opening up to be identical with true purity. Since form and mind appear vividly, the three contemplations are simultaneously illuminated; first, one contemplates with the contemplation of emptiness.

The form and mind of sentient beings and Buddhas suddenly become identical to the True Aspect of Emptiness and are pure; contemplate this with the Contemplation of the Conventional (Jiaguān), and the form and mind of sentient beings and Buddhas suddenly become identical to the Conventional Aspect and are pure.
Contemplate this with the Contemplation of the Middle (Zhongguān), and the form and mind of sentient beings and Buddhas suddenly become identical to the Middle Aspect and are pure.
This is because when the three contemplations are simultaneously applied, at the very place where form and mind are manifest, one is able to...

It causes form and mind to suddenly open up and become identical with the true principle of the three truths; furthermore, "and pure" also suddenly opens up to be identical with true purity. (The phrase "one sentence belongs to the subsequent explanation.

Moreover, the meaning of this passage—that the substance of form and mind is utterly severed and is solely the one real nature—is spoken in terms of counteractive treatment (*pratipakṣa*) to shatter former attachments;
thus, it causes one to see purely the single nature within form and mind, so that while form and mind remain distinct, they suddenly open up and become identical with the True.

As for "purity," if one perceives the single nature, then one perceives that this single nature is purely composed of form and mind. △ Second, the explanation of the two [aspects]: first, the explanation of "extinction.
There are no longer the distinctions of sentient beings or the seven stages of skillful means, nor does one perceive the differences between pure and impure lands.
Therefore, this passage explains the loss of the characteristics of both the primary and secondary retributions (*niśraya-vastu*). "Sentient beings" refers to the primary retribution;

because it universally encompasses the loss of all ten realms, it says there are "no more sentient beings. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The supreme among sentient beings is the Buddha. Thus, one knows that "sentient beings" includes all ten realms.
Because the three vehicles are specifically singled out, it speaks of the "seven stages of expedient means" (*saptavidha-upāya*) as distinct from them. Furthermore, it mentions the "land" (*kṣetra*).
The phrase "the one who speaks" refers to the dependent retribution (依報). Because it universally transcends the four lands, it is said that "no lands are seen";
because it specifically addresses purity and defilement, it is said that "purity and defilement differ in degree. △ Second, the explanation of illumination.
Yet the celestial net of Indra, consisting of both the environment and its inhabitants, remains ultimately self-luminous;
this is used as an analogy to illustrate manifest illumination. △ Second, the explanation of the internal [reality] has two parts. First, realizing the external and returning to the internal:
Regarding what is called "internal," one first realizes that the external forms and mind are, in a single thought-moment, devoid of thought.
From the deluded state of meditative concentration, there is a distinction between internal and external; yet, regarding awakening as contemplation, internal and external are identical.

Thus, one knows that form and mind are entirely a single thought-moment, equal in their very place. Since even internal thought ceases, it is called "no-thought. △ Second, explaining the characteristics with respect to the internal.
The three thousand realms within the internal essence are themselves emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.

Because the internal essence is one's own mind and the three thousand realms of delusory objects are what is manifested as the three truths, they are said to be "identical to emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.

Furthermore, the three thousand realms within the internal essence are dharmas produced by causes and conditions; when these conditionally produced phenomena are pointed out, they are precisely the principle of the three truths.

Therefore, it is said that "emptiness, the provisional, and the middle are identical. When various texts state that the three thousand [dharmas] are "identical to emptiness, the provisional, and the middle," or simply "identical to emptiness" and "identical to the middle," or simply "the provisional," what is the answer?

First, one must understand the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of the three thousand dharmas before one can recognize the intended application—whether advancing or regressing—of these various texts. This is because the three thousand cannot be established through principle alone, nor through phenomena alone.
If these are not fully possessed, one must first integrate the phenomena of the ten realms through the principle of emptiness;

only then do the realms and their suchness mutually possess one another, which is what is called the "three thousand. Therefore, the substance of the three thousand penetrates the three truths. Within these three thousand, there are emptiness, the provisional, and the middle;
by taking up their substance as a whole, they are called the "three thousand. Because the substance points to the possession of all virtues, they are named emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.
In a certain text, after enumerating the three thousand [realms], it further states that these are "immediately empty, provisional, and middle. I ask:
within these three thousand, which phenomena are the empty and the middle, and which phenomena are the conventional and the provisional? Answer:

Within the three thousand, if one takes up even a single phenomenon, it immediately encompasses the entirety of the empty, the provisional, and the middle. For example, taking up a "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) is the provisional; this characteristic is itself...
Because the characteristic [of existence] is for the sake of emptiness, the characteristic itself is integrated with it; therefore, this characteristic already possesses emptiness within it.

The above has been explained in terms of the three thousand dharmas as the essence of reality, which encompasses all things without exception and is fully endowed with emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.

If one takes the principle of emptiness within the middle and integrates it with the phenomena of the ten realms, the three thousand [realms] are thereby established. Thus, that which is able to establish these is the "emptiness" (the noumenal), and that which is established therein is the "conventional" (the phenomenal).
Since the "phenomenon" (the fact) is set aside and only that which is accomplished is taken up, the three thousand realms are exclusively conventional.

For this reason, various texts may refer to the three thousand realms as being solely "provisional" (*prajñapti*); this is because there is nothing among those things accomplished that is not conventional.

Within this conventionality, there are further two directions: the first takes this very conventionality as being identical to its nature, and is therefore termed "non-... [implying non-arising/non-perishing].

If conventional reality were as you conceive it, then merely mentioning the "three thousand" would already constitute the wondrous provisional; therefore, we simply say it is "identical with emptiness and identical with the middle.
If one were to further say it is "identical with the provisional," it would become redundant and cumbersome. As the *Yili* (Exemplification of Meaning) states:

"Observing this single movement, it immediately possesses the ten realms, the hundred realms, and the thousand suchnesses; 'identical with emptiness' and 'identical with the middle' both take this conventional reality as their basis. Although this is so...
Setting aside its essential nature for the moment, we consider only its conventional aspect; yet this conventionality is precisely dependent origination.

Furthermore, this dependent origination encompasses two meanings: first, because it is derived from the very substance of phenomena, the conventional of dependent origination is identical in substance to the inconceivable conventional within the Three Truths.
Since their substances are identical, the mention of dependent origination itself already [establishes this].

Regarding the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it is likewise said to be "identical with emptiness" and "identical with the Middle. When these two are distinguished according to their respective meanings, there are further two senses:

the conventional as dependently arisen is distinct from the wondrous provisional; yet again, there are two senses. If the conventional does not immediately coincide with nature, it is termed "dependently arisen" and is not the three thousand [realms].
If the conventional immediately coincides with nature, it is the three thousand [realms] and is not "dependently arisen," but belongs to the wondrous provisional.
As stated in the *Yili* (Exemplification of Meaning): "To contemplate this single movement is precisely dependent origination;

that it encompasses the ten realms, the hundred realms, and the thousandfold suchness is precisely the wondrous provisional. It further states: "Although one contemplates the ten realms and the four movements, these are dependent origination;
when realms and movements are both forgotten and one contemplates only the three thousand [realms], this is the wondrous provisional. Although these two are...

The "three thousand" are also called "dependently originated"; thus, having first presented the three thousand as dependently originated conventional reality, one then points out that these very three thousand dependently originated phenomena are themselves the Three Truths.
Therefore, it is further stated that they are "identical with emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. As the *Miaofa Lianhua Jing Xuan Yi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra) says:
"When the ten realms interact, there are a thousand phenomena; such phenomena as these are all dharmas produced by causes and conditions."
"Up to this point, I have taught that what is emptiness is also called the provisional name, and is also called the meaning of the Middle Way. Question:

"Is the arising conditioned by the three thousand fetters conceivable (*cintya*) or inconceivable (*acintya*)? Answer: "The essence of phenomena has but a single name that extends toward two directions.
However, because we take up the aspect of 'arising through conditions,' it is conceivable. If one takes up the fact that arising through conditions is such that [the factors] are mutually..."
Because it possesses these qualities, it is inconceivable. As the *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) states:
"If one contemplates that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) arises through causes and conditions, such that a single aspect contains all aspects," this is designated as the inconceivable.

Although it is inconceivable, because it is grasped as arising from conditions, the *Zhiguan* further points to the three truths. One may ask: how is it known that [this] applies universally to the conventional truth of dependent origination?

These two meanings are answered based on the *Zhiguan* (Mo-ho chih-kuan), which states: "Phenomena produced by causes and conditions are themselves emptiness and themselves the Middle. The commentary explains:
"To speak merely of 'emptiness and the Middle' is to provisionally describe the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)—emptiness and the Middle—in contrast to illusory conventionality;

in reality, one must say that illusory conventionality is itself the inconceivable conventionality" (this constitutes two sections based on a difference in meaning). Why is this? Because here we rely solely upon this...
The conventional (*saṃvṛti*) is itself emptiness (*śūnyatā*); because this convention is spontaneously established as the inconceivable (*acintya*), it is not explained separately.

This is based on their identity in essence (*tattva-samāna*), being merely a single convention; yet, because they differ in terms of "being identical" versus "not being identical," they are divided into two distinct categories.

Now, taking their identity in essence, there is no separate inconceivable convention; rather, one simply points to dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as being itself emptiness. Thus, this dependent...
This generates the "wondrous provisional" (*miaojia*). However, the meaning of this passage is profound and obscure, difficult to comprehend;

one should seek within the text the two instances where it says, "this provisional [nature] manifests itself," which explains that while their meanings differ, their substance is identical. Many scholars have asked:

since the two substances of the "partial provisional" (*pianjia*) and the "wondrous provisional" (*miaojia*) are distinct, and the partial and the perfect (*yuan*) are naturally separate, does this not mean that the partial provisional is refuted in order to manifest the wondrous provisional? It is simply because of the Perfect [Teaching].

Since the central point is to refute [the opponent] by means of the treatise itself, throughout the various passages, the focus is exclusively on dependent origination as the perfect and subtle [truth].
To employ "provisional" (jia) as an auxiliary term is precisely this intention. If one asks: "If the two provisional [truths] are identical in essence, why does the text say 'in reality' (qishi)?
The answer is: regarding the claim that the essences of the two provisional truths differ, from ancient times there have been two differing views. First...

It is said that "dependent origination" is the characteristic of existence, while "wondrous conventionality" is its nature and not its characteristic. Alternatively, it is said that "dependent origination" is the characteristic of the sentient being, while "wondrous conventionality" is the characteristic of the faculties.
Now, I maintain that the former statement merely identifies the nature of the possessing subject as wondrous conventionality, and thus may be described as "not a characteristic.
As for the latter statement, it errs regarding the essential body of the possessed phenomenon; it is simply one and the same.
What is this? For instance, when Mount Sumeru enters a mustard seed, it must necessarily be through the retribution obtained by humans and devas;
yet it is the wondrous function of all Buddhas that Mount Sumeru possesses two kinds of Sumeru-substance. Seeking it through this, there is only one Sumeru.
Because this Sumeru has not yet entered into emptiness, it is not the "wondrous provisional"; as soon as it enters into emptiness, then—

Regarding the statement that "the wondrous provisional [truth] cannot have two distinct entities," the text says, "As for its reality (*tattva*)," which refers to a difference in meaning based on its own context.

The intent is that since the meanings of the two types of provisional [truths] differ, their reality must be described as: "conditioned phenomena arising from causes and conditions are themselves emptiness and themselves the provisional.
However, if one considers them identical in terms of their essence (*svabhāva*), it can also be said that "the illusory provisional is itself the wondrous provisional."
As asked in the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary): "This inconceivable [teaching] is explained through the sequence [of the ten realms];

how does it differ from the conceivable? The answer is: in reality, there is no difference. The conceivable is explained as arising from the mind, whereas the inconceivable is explained as the single mind being fully possessed [of all].
Since the inconceivable uses "arising" to manifest "possession," why ask again about the arising of the mind? Is this not the same as the illusory and provisional?
"How can the mind's possession [of all things] not be identical to the wondrous mundane? (etc. △ Third, the conclusion on non-duality. Part one: the specific conclusion.
First, concluding by subsuming the external within the internal:
"Thus, external phenomena are entirely the nature of the mind; the nature of the mind has no exterior, and its subsumption is all-pervasive."

By means of one's own mind-nature, one can encompass the sentient beings and the Buddha-realm, including both the physical environment (*rūpa*) and its inhabitants (*citta*). △ Second, concluding by showing that the external encompasses the internal:
the nature and essence of the Buddhas of the ten directions and all sentient beings within the *dharmadhātu* are without distinction; all are universally permeated.

Since the essence of the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is no different from the essence of one's own nature, and since one's own nature already encompasses the natures of both sentient beings and Buddhas, the essence of the Buddha-nature of sentient beings likewise encompasses one's own body and environment, as well as their physical and mental faculties; therefore, it is said that "all things are universally pervaded.
△ Second, the general conclusion.
Who says there are internal and external, form and mind, self and other?
Since one has already subsumed all within the nature of one's own mind, there is nothing outside the Buddhas and sentient beings; thus, there is no "external.

Furthermore, since one has subsumed the nature of the minds of sentient beings and Buddhas within oneself, there is nothing inside; thus, there is no "internal. When internal and external have both vanished, how can there be self and other?
△ Three Bonds. This is established by means of the aforementioned "Gate of the Non-duality of Matter and Mind.

Matter and mind are established as external and internal based on their objects; they are discussed in terms of wisdom and practice based on their support. Since wisdom is generated from the object, [the three bonds] are thus formed.

It is said that this employs the preceding discussion of form and mind (*rūpa-citta*). Furthermore, while the previous section discussed form and mind by way of the three dharmas, the present discussion distinguishes the three dharmas by way of form and mind; therefore, it is said that they are "established. △ First, the heading.
Regarding the "Gate of the Non-duality of the Threefold Nature of Cultivation":
this gate takes the single, equal nature as the essence of non-duality. Because the nature of the object and the contemplation of that object are identical, it is discussed as non-dual.
Therefore, the text below states: "One realizes that the nature of cultivation is non-existent, being solely the wondrous vehicle; by means of equality..."
Because the nature of equality (*samatā*) constitutes the essence of the vehicle, its objects and contemplations each possess both an innate (*prakṛti*) and a cultivated (*bhāvanā*) aspect:

the three thousand realms as inherent in nature constitute the innate object, while the three thousand realms as functioning through cultivation constitute the cultivated object; the three contemplations as inherent in nature constitute the innate contemplation, while the three contemplations as cultivated virtues constitute the cultivated contemplation.

Question: Since the objects and contemplations have already been discussed within the "internal" and "external" sections above, how do they differ from those presented here? Answer: Regarding the internal...

Although the external encompasses both object and contemplation, it remains on the side of intellectual understanding of the object; since one has not yet engaged in actual practice, it differs from the present [stage].

△ Second, the explanation of the two [aspects]: first, the indication of the two; first, the characteristics of the cultivated nature (bhāvanā-dhātu); first, the general indication; first, the indication of the cultivated nature.

The nature-virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*) are simply the *dharmadhātu*; within a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), these three dharmas are fully present. Although the nature is thus from the beginning, it relies upon wisdom to initiate cultivation.
Furthermore, the nature of the four virtues is nothing other than the *dharmadhātu*, and this *dharmadhātu* resides precisely within this single thought-moment. This thought-moment...

The middle realm (*madhyadhātu*) is like the three virtues (*triguṇa*) and the three tracks (*trivartman*), for there is nothing that is not perfectly complete; hence it is said that this internal realm is fully endowed with the three dharmas.

"Internal" (*neng*) here means "middle" (*madhya*); it is a term used to refer to the dharma, differing from the "internal" (*neng*) of the previous passage regarding the internal objects (*adhyātmaviṣaya*).

Although the nature of these objects inherently possesses the three [virtues], they must rely on the power of wisdom to give rise to their cultivated nature. Thus, the objects are three, which are precisely the dharmas.

Because there are three within the body, it is said they are "primordially so" (*bennyō*); because wisdom arises in dependence upon objects, these are the three aspects of wisdom (*chi*), which are the three [aspects] within *prajñā*.
Because one relies on wisdom and is guided by wisdom in practice, these are the three aspects of conduct (*gyō*), which are the three [aspects] within liberation (*gedatsu*).

Thus it is said: "arising cultivation. This "arising cultivation" refers to these three aspects of nature (*shōsan*); because they are illuminated by wisdom, one gives rise to and advances toward them. This is...
The accomplishment and cultivation [of these] will be explained below as appropriate. △ Second, the exegesis through transformation:

Because one cultivates the illumination of the nature, this serves as the exegesis for how cultivation arises by relying on wisdom. Why is this excellent? It is because this cultivation is able to illuminate the nature.
Cultivation arises from the nature.
To further explain: although the nature is inherently so, if the nature were not complete, how could cultivation arise?
When one abides in the nature, cultivation is entirely perfected as the nature.
To further explain how cultivation is generated by means of the nature (*prakṛti*): what is it that the nature can generate?
It is simply because, while one abides in the state of the nature, the entirety of cultivation is perfected as that very nature; therefore, this nature generates cultivation.
When cultivation arises, the entire nature becomes cultivation.
To explain further: why is it that cultivation can illuminate the nature? It is precisely because at the time cultivation arises, the entire nature constitutes cultivation;
therefore, this cultivation is able to illuminate the nature.
The nature does not shift.

When one explains that cultivation arises through transformation, it means that the nature is entirely realized as cultivation; yet once cultivation is accomplished, should it not follow that the nature no longer exists?
One should know that although cultivation is thus accomplished, the nature undergoes no alteration whatsoever.
Cultivation remains ever-vivid. To explain further:
if cultivation is entirely perfected within the nature (*prakṛti*), then once it has become the nature, would there not be no further cultivation?

One should know that although it has become the nature, cultivation itself remains perfectly vivid. △ Second, the specific demonstration of the two [aspects]: first, the demonstration of the inverse and the compliant. First...
The demonstration.
Furthermore, cultivation (bhāvanā) is of two kinds: cultivation in accordance with the sequence (anuloma-bhāvanā) and cultivation in reverse order (pratiloma-bhāvanā).
△ Second, the explanation of the five [aspects], beginning with the two meanings of reverse and direct order.
"Conformity" means realizing one's nature as practice; "rebellion" means turning one's back on that nature to become deluded.

First, regarding the distinction between rebellion and conformity based on the essence of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas: from the ultimate perspective, the nine realms are rebellious, while cultivating the Buddha-realm is conforming.
The natural, innate body-and-mind fundamentally possesses both good and evil; when it possesses goodness, it is the Buddha.
The ten realms in their natural order are termed "enlightenment," while the ten realms in their reverse order are termed "delusion.
These two are distinguished as either inverse or conformative, and as either evil or good, based on whether one knows or does not know [the nature of reality].

Since the ten realms are inherently possessed by nature, when they are manifested through cultivation, one who can fully realize that the cultivation of good and evil is entirely inherent in nature is said to be "conformative enlightenment"; one who does not so realize is deluded.
The cultivation of good and evil that arises from the perfection of one's nature is called "contrary delusion. Question:
It is understandable to call the realization of good "conformity," but how can the realization of evil also be called "conformity"? Answer: It is only for fear that one does not realize it;

if one were to realize it, evil would be entirely the nature itself, and one would see that the essence of nature is fundamentally neither good nor evil. Therefore, it is called "conformity. Those who transmit the teachings of Siming all say this.

To cultivate evil as being merely the nature of evil, and to take this very evil as the substance of contemplation, is to fail to realize that one must penetrate the darkness of cultivated evil to perceive the brightness of cultivated good. This is because both delusion and wisdom are identical to the nature.
Therefore, not only is the nature of delusion no different [from the nature of wisdom], but even delusion and wisdom themselves are of one essence; thus, it is attained.

It is said that when one realizes that the observing wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) is itself ignorance (*avidyā*), and that these two—characteristic and essence—are simultaneously identical, only then can it be said that evil is the essence of observation.
Jingxi [Zhiyi] said: "If one has not yet even heard the name of 'inherently evil nature,' how could one believe in the practice of 'inherent virtuous nature'?
This does not mean that evil is taken as the practice of inherent virtue; rather, it refers to the nature itself.
The practice of virtue is a wholesome conduct based on three causes. Because it is unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*), it is called "intrinsic virtue" (*prakṛti-guṇa*).

This is because such conduct is not merely a matter of cultivation through its own substance; rather, it is the nature itself, and is therefore termed "unconditioned. As for the evil that is to be abandoned, evil itself is the nature and there is nothing to be abandoned.
Thus, the practice capable of abandoning [evil] is named "unconditioned," thereby manifesting it by means of that which is to be remedied.

Since the nature of both that which can treat [the afflictions] and that which is to be treated as evil is thus established, one may trust that the practice capable of treating them is likewise identical to this nature.
What is called "evil nature" refers to the three realms of cyclic existence (*trivartman*) mentioned in the preceding text;

what is called "nature-practice" (*xing-xing*) refers to the three causes for cultivating virtue mentioned in the preceding text. Because the provisional is opened up, reality is seen within the provisional.

Therefore, the three paths and the three causes are all termed "nature" (*xing*). Thus, it can be said that the nature-virtues (*xingde*) possess both the conditions (*yuan*) and the understanding (*liao*).
△ Second, the delusion and understanding of nature are identical, yet the phenomena of opposition and compliance differ.
Although the two minds of delusion and understanding are not dual, the two natures of opposition and compliance are eternally distinct in both their essence and their manifestations.
The two minds that are deluded are precisely the deluded mind; they are merely the "mind that can delude" and the "mind that can discern," both of which are the ignorant mind.
Although these two minds are not distinct, when one points to this deluded mind, it is itself the true principle; therefore, they are called non-dual.
The two natures of opposition and compliance are themselves the true nature; for the nature of True Suchness (Tathatā) is that which is opposed and that which is complied with.

Regarding these two natures, the fact that their essential nature (*svabhāva*) and their phenomenal activity (*vastu*) are eternally distinct means that their true nature serves as the basis for both adverse and favorable activities;

thus they are said to be "eternally distinct. Furthermore, the superior mind is delusion while the inferior mind is truth; because the deluded mind is pointed out as being the true mind, they are said to be "non-dual.
The superior nature is truth while the inferior nature is delusion; because the true nature is transformed into a deluded nature, they are said to be "eternal[ly distinct]."
Extraordinary. △ Third, if one does not reform their delusion and rebellion, there is no way for completion to be achieved.
Since it is through the mind that affairs do not shift, one must cause the practice of delusion to reach completion.
To cause the practice of delusion to reach completion, one must necessarily transform rebellion and return to obedience; how could one possibly achieve this while rebellious affairs remain unaltered?
This causes the deluded mind to achieve completion. △ Fourth, transforming the contrary into the compliant.
Therefore, throughout one period of time, one must transform delusion into awakening, illumination into nature, and cultivation into realization.
"Period" refers to the span from the initial stage of names and words to the ultimate stage; within this single period, it is necessary in all cases to turn delusion into completion.
"By means of clearly understanding delusion, one causes delusion to be identical with nature; by illuminating nature, cultivation is perfected.

Regarding the question of how the single gate of the identity of cultivation and nature can encompass both the two subtleties of wisdom and practice: "clearly understanding delusion" is the subtlety of wisdom, while "illuminating nature to perfect cultivation" is the subtlety of practice.
Since these do not yet constitute the subtlety of stages, how can they explain the perfection of cultivation through the understanding of delusion as extending all the way to the ultimate?
Answer: Because they arise from the text, they reside within the contemplation of names; their high and deep significance must encompass the six identities (*ṣaḍ-yukti*).

Principle itself is that which is understood, while names and so forth are the means by which they are understood. Regarding names: through the transformation of delusion via understanding, one achieves the five grades;

through the transformation of delusion via practice, one achieves [the stages] up to the ultimate Buddha, who perfectly illuminates the nature to complete cultivation. This cultivation is ultimately perfected.

Although this is the general discourse, if we discuss it specifically: "wisdom" (*jñāna*) refers to realization, while "practice" (*caryā*) refers to cultivation; since cultivation belongs to the sublime conduct (*sucarita*), this passage precisely clarifies the nature of cultivation.
Some may claim that "one" (*yi*) should be interpreted as "to unify," but in either case, these do not accord with the meaning of the text.
△ Fifth: Both the inverse and the conforming are transcended.

When the two minds of seeing the nature and cultivating the mind both subside, if one can see the nature through both adverse and favorable conditions, the nature is fundamentally non-existent and has subsided; how then could there be further delusion or awakening?
△ Second, showing the separation and union [of the two], first: the general heading.
Furthermore, it is explained that the cultivation of the nature of correspondence (pratipakṣa-bhāvanā) involves both separation and conjunction.

Some maintain that "separation" signifies individuality—meaning that the cultivated nature consists of three distinct elements each—and that "conjunction" signifies correspondence—meaning that because the cultivated nature is made clear through correspondence, the two cultivations are joined together. Now, I say that both "correspondence" and "individuality" equally encompass both separation and conjunction.

Regarding the correlation between the "correspondence" (duì) and the "separation/combination" (líhé): since it is said that one practices in accordance with the nature of correspondence, there is both separation and combination.

Is separation not itself a form of correspondence? When each possesses its own separation and combination, "separation" refers to what others cite as distinct; "each corresponding and combining" refers to what the *Myōki* states:

"Therefore, the three natures are collectively bound together as the single causal conditions of the direct cause, the object-condition, and the enabling condition; their respective combinations and unions are termed 'one'. △ Second, the specific explanation.
Regarding the second [section], there are two parts: first, the three dharmas; second, the three, six, and two [categories] of the treatise concerning their separation and combination.
"Separation" means that the cultivated (*bhāvanā*) and the innate (*prakṛti*) each have three types. "Combination" means that the cultivated has two types and the innate has one.

However, regarding these cultivated and innate [qualities], the text states that the second and third [categories] are established based on wisdom and conduct; therefore, they are explained as being cultivated.

The nature [of these categories] is all established through the combination and separation of the three aspects of object (*ālambana*), wisdom (*jñāna*), and practice (*caryā*). That is to say, each attains its own basis.

As for the passage in the *Xuánqiān* (Profound Commentary) that fully cites the "three objects, three wisdoms, and three practices" to explain the present combination and separation, I fear this may not be the case.

One should know that when the two gates of the internal and external, as well as the cultivated and the innate (*bhāvanā-prakṛti*), are discussed in general terms, each possesses wisdom and practice. Regarding the internal and external gates, it says: [text continues].

"Are all observed objects not comprised of the internal and external, and thus not the practice? Furthermore, it is said: 'First, one realizes that external forms are, in a single thought-moment, non-thought;
this realization is not wisdom. In the Section on Cultivation and Nature, it says: 'Conformity means taking nature as practice, which is precisely wisdom; practice is precisely practice.
If explained according to their specific distinctions, the categories of internal and external are each distinct, residing respectively in wisdom and the sublime."

Regarding the section distinguishing the cultivated nature (*xiùxìng*) from the inherent nature (*xìngxìng*) within the internal and external, this distinction lies specifically in the excellence of practice (*xíngmiào*). As for how this is so:

it is because the text states that although the nature is originally thus, one relies upon wisdom to initiate cultivation. This implies that by relying on the excellence of wisdom, one initiates the excellence of practice;
therefore, it is the excellence of practice that is designated as "cultivation. Thus, the cultivation of the excellence of practice is contrasted with the reality of the realms (*jièrú*).

Therefore, the principle establishes the "Gate of the Non-duality of Cultivation and Nature. By this one may verify that although [the category of] "wondrous wisdom" encompasses all, when distinguishing between cultivation and nature, it must pertain to "wondrous practice.

Thus, throughout this gate from beginning to end, with the exception of the character *xiū* (cultivate) used in the term *nìxiū* (counter-cultivation), every other instance of the character *xiū* refers to wondrous practice. Question: Is wisdom not cultivation? Answer: Wisdom is a designation; in comparison to...

The principle-as-such (*ri-ji*) also belongs to cultivation; however, it constitutes cultivation only in the sense of intellectual understanding, not as the cultivation of contemplative practice (*guan-xing*).

Now, when we distinguish between cultivation and nature, we are referring specifically to the cultivation of contemplative practice; therefore, one must separately designate the "wonderful practice" (*xing-miao*) as cultivation.

If one were to say otherwise, how could one reconcile the fact that the text merely states that "one relies on wisdom to initiate cultivation," clearly indicating that wisdom itself is not taken as cultivation? It is untenable.
If one practices by means of conduct from within the interval of strength, is this not the same as the objection raised by the *Zhengyi*? Answer:
The *Zhengyi* does not intend to change "wisdom" (*zhì*) into "knowledge" (*zhī*). Its meaning is that, according to the current text, wisdom is taken as cultivation;

if one understands the current text such that conduct constitutes cultivation and it is not changed, then one should question the intent of the text. The *Zhengyi*’s objection states: "When wisdom arises... [and so forth].

Question: If one cultivates this [wisdom], is it not the case that wisdom itself is also cultivated? Answer: My point is that your words merely embellish the text while your meaning still falls into the same difficulty.
Why? Regarding what you say—that when wisdom arises, it is cultivation—this single term "cultivation" (xiū): is it wisdom or is it practice (xing)?
If you say it is wisdom, it contradicts the fact that the character for "cultivation" in the text refers to practice; therefore, it is said that one "relies upon wisdom."
And yet, [the text] speaks of "arising in cultivation. If one says this is "practice" (xing), then it actually establishes what is called "excellent practice" as being "cultivation" (xiu).
Therefore, we know that this passage is precisely discussing the stages (*wei*) in a vertical sense; one must not insist on taking it as a horizontal classification to raise an objection.

(As stated above. Yuan Tong said: "Jingxi’s language is skillful and must be properly understood. He intends to subsume the three categories of object, wisdom, and practice under the two terms 'cultivation' and 'nature' (xing)."
Therefore, it is said that although nature (*xing*) is fundamentally thus, one relies on wisdom (*zhi*) to initiate cultivation (*xiu*).
The reason why it is not said that one relies on wisdom to initiate practice (*xing*) lies precisely in this intention. Now, I say this is not so;

if it were as others claim, it would conversely result in the statement by Jingxi being clumsy. Why? Because if one wishes to subsume both wisdom and practice within cultivation, one may simply speak [of them as such].
The phrase "relying on wisdom to give rise to practice" responds to the previous statement that "the nature is originally thus. Therefore, wisdom and practice can both be taken as cultivation;

why then speak separately of the practice that arises [from wisdom] as being the "arising of cultivation"? Is this not merely a clever turn of phrase? Question: Is wisdom not something apart from [the distinction between] separation and union?

Answer: Wisdom is subtle and indeed discerns both separation and union. As the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning) states regarding the object (*viṣaya*): [it discerns whether it is separated from or united with the subject].
The three types of wisdom based on principle are identical to the three practices based on names; the three practices based on contemplation are identical to the three practices based on semblance.

One should know that these nine are merely three sets of three, and these three are merely one. However, in the present text, the distinction between their separation and combination is made by correlating the three practices based on application with the three objects.
Question: Is there wisdom without practice? Answer: When discussed vertically according to stages, wisdom belongs to the stage of names, while practice is sublime.
This belongs to the stage of semblance within contemplative practice; therefore, while the practice is wondrous, it is not yet wisdom (*prajñā*).

When analyzing the practices horizontally according to the Dharma, although *prajñā* exists within the midst of those wondrous practices, is it not indeed wisdom? However, this wisdom is entirely subsumed under "practice";
thus, one may say that based on the wondrousness of practice, it is termed "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*). By discerning their separation and conjunction, one understands this meaning.
Having thus explained it, the meanings of the cultivation and nature (śikṣā-prakṛti), their separation and union, are all perfectly consistent.

There are three aspects each for both cultivation and nature; because there are three aspects of nature and three aspects of cultivation, they are said to be "three each. This refers to the six phenomena (*ṣaḍ-dharma*) characterized by the subtle practice (*caryā-māhātmya*), wherein the three aspects of cultivation correspond to the three aspects of the realms as they are (*yathābhūta*) within the three aspects of nature—thus, three natures and three cultivations. Regarding "two cultivations and one nature," this is due to the subtle practice.

The third [classification] is designated by its predominant factor: although it consists of the cultivation of both *prajñā* (wisdom) and liberation (*vimukti*), it is named "cultivation" because the *dharmakāya* is the primary object of this practice.

The second [classification] is designated by its predominant factor: although it consists of the *dharmakāya* as the nature (*svabhāva*) and the *prajñā* and liberation within that object, it is named "nature" because the *dharmakāya* is the fundamental essence.
For a single person, there are three [aspects] based on the object and three based on the wisdoms.

Regarding the explanation of the three aspects of practice as being distinct from [the three aspects of nature]: there are two points that cannot be accepted. First, the current text states that "there are three each for both nature and practice.
Is the single character *xiū* (practice) here not the same as the character *xiū* (practice) from the preceding passage, which spoke of "relying on wisdom to give rise to practice"?
How can one now explain the three aspects of wisdom as being distinct from the two aspects of practice? If this were already the case in the current text...

Regarding the cultivation of the six natures—three of which are also mentioned below in the section on the cultivation of the two [natures] each with three—and their common arousal of the three innate natures (*prakṛti-prativedha*), how is the wording of these passages distinct?
It is not meant as a redundant explanation. △ Second, the analysis of combination and separation according to the *Triṃśikā-bhāṣya*.

The two types of cultivation each have three aspects, which together with the three aspects of the nature that they jointly arouse—these constitute the ninefold cultivation. Although there are nine, they are merely three;
this is because the cultivation is presented as a pair in contrast to the nature, and thus the two cultivations are combined into one.

Others say that the two cultivations each have three aspects, while the nature that they jointly arouse has three aspects, explaining the meaning of "separation" mentioned above. However, I say this is not so; regarding the aforementioned...

Setting aside these [distinctions], there are three each for the cultivated (*bhāvanā*) and the innate (*prakṛti*). Now, setting aside these, within the cultivated there are nine, because of the mistaken identification of six as nine;
thus, the explanation of the meaning of the following passage becomes inconsistent with the text. Why is this?

In reality, the three practices (*caryā*) mentioned in the preceding text are the objects of cultivation, while the three are the innate; thus, when separated, cultivation and nature each have three, but when combined, cultivation has only two.

The nature (xing) is merely a single category, while the meaning of "cultivation" (xiu) refers to the comprehensive discussion of the three [categories] and the six [subdivisions], including their separation and combination.

In the present text, regarding cultivation there are only two [categories], each of which further possesses three; thus, they constitute the six of cultivation. Because these six of cultivation illuminate and bring forth the three of nature, nature also belongs to cultivation.
Therefore, it is said that although cultivation possesses nine when separated, and although nature possesses nine when combined, [the principle remains as stated].
Regarding the statement that "nine" refers to three: these are simply the three [natures], for they are discussed in terms of the cultivation of the nine by way of their combination and separation.

Thus, this differs from the two meanings mentioned in the preceding text. First, while the preceding text discusses both cultivation and nature generally, the present text speaks solely in terms of cultivation.
Although the discussion here encompasses nature, it is subsumed under cultivation; for through the two aspects of cultivation, six dharmas are distinguished, which in turn bring forth nature.
Therefore, while the preceding passage concerns the characteristics of the three sets of six dharmas, the present passage concerns the characteristics of the three sets of nine dharmas.

Nevertheless, regarding the principle of separation and combination: from the perspective of their names, the paths of separation and combination differ; yet from the perspective of their essential meaning, the general and the specific are unified.

Furthermore, when discussed comprehensively, they possess all attributes and thus are separated; when considered specifically according to their functional application, they are combined. This is as detailed in the separate chapter. △ Second, the analogies.
The two and the one-nature are like water being waves; the two are non-dual, just as waves and water are.
The one-nature is illustrated by water, and the two practices are illustrated by waves. The complete one-nature constitutes the two practices;

apart from the complete water, there is no nature of the waves. Having realized that the two practices are the one-nature, there is no practice apart from that nature, just as there is no water apart from the waves.

Waves are understood to be water because there is no wave apart from water; therefore, it is said that "the two are also non-dual. This is like the analogy of waves and water, where the word "also" (*yi*) is used for both the dharma (the subject) and the metaphor (the example) to compare their natures.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the nature of the two and the one" mentioned above, the first instance of the character "two" (*er*) refers to the two aspects of cultivation;
regarding the phrase "the two are also non-dual" mentioned below, the second instance of the character "two" (*er*) [refers to the two aspects of the result].
The preceding section on the mutual identity of cultivation and nature uses the analogy of water and waves—water being the waves and waves being the water.
The following section discusses the dissolution of the essence of cultivation and nature: because waves are water, there are no waves; because water is waves, there is no water.
Thus it is said that both are non-dual, just as with waves and water. △ Second, the locus of cultivation and nature.

From [the perspective of] nature (*dhātu*), one should know that it refers to the three obstacles; therefore, by means of the three cultivations based on nature, the three dharmas are accomplished as their natural result (*dharmatā*).
This passage should refer to the nature, the three cultivations, and the three results, which can never be described as "this cultivation" being three, or as two cultivations each [being distinct].
Third, the three natures arise from the three obstacles, and the three practices arise from the three natures.
If one returns the practices to the natures and the natures to delusion, one will suddenly awaken to the true source, which is vast and empty, with nothing upon which to rely.
Is this not because the substance of the single nature is fundamentally not three, yet the source possessed by the nature-body is discussed through the delusions produced by duality?
It is then said that these three are "phrases of radiant light": where there is a phenomenon (shi), there must be its principle (li);
since both phenomenon and principle exist, there must necessarily be that which is neither phenomenon nor principle. These three dharmas all arise from ignorance. Furthermore, the *Jinbi* states:
"From beginningless time, you have possessed nothing but afflictions, karma, and suffering; yet these are entirely the three causes of the rational nature."
The *Wenyintongzhiyao* states: "Question: Since the three natures are fundamentally complete, why are they said to be named 'three' in relation to obstacles? Answer:
If the fundamentally complete wondrous principle were fixedly three, it could not function as one or as the infinite. Therefore, we know that when established, the one and the many are distinct;
when extinguished, cultivation and nature are quiescent. Since we are currently speaking from the perspective of extinction, how can one employ the perspective of establishment?"
If one challenges this by asking why the intent is not explicitly stated— namely, that the three natures of the obstacles are established only when they are fully present,
rather than saying they are absent in the deceased— is there not a profound purpose? It must be that because the wondrous principle of nature is fundamentally quiescent and transcendent,
such that not a single dharma can be established as a discrete entity, one is then able to be simultaneously one, three, and immeasurable.

Therefore, it is said that the three natures are established based on their discourse. Furthermore, if one were to speak merely of the "three," one would only capture the function of the nature while losing the essence of the nature. △ Second, the conclusion on non-duality.
Reaching the state where there is no nature of cultivation, there is only the single wondrous vehicle; the dharma-realm is transparently luminous, free from all discrimination.
When both cultivation and nature are forgotten, all return to equality; yet if there is discrimination, the dharma-realm becomes delusion. △ Third, the conclusion.
This is established through the gate of the non-duality of the internal and external.

While the general process of arising from the text clarifies that both the cultivation and the nature of the internal and external arise from wisdom and practice, the gates of cultivation and nature are established based on the internal and external;
yet, if explained specifically and distinctly, the internal is wisdom and the nature of the external is practice.

Because wisdom establishes practice, one is able to accomplish this. If we distinguish between the internal and external from the perspective of intention, although there is a single gateway where object and contemplation correspond to cultivation and nature, these are merely the objects of the three dharmas that are known. To distinguish non-duality, it belongs to the present category of "nature.
Now, because we wish to harmonize the non-duality of object and contemplation, the question is established next: surely object and wisdom have not yet [merged]?

How much more so since the three thousand realms of delusion in the cause and the three thousand realms of awakening in the fruit are both unchanging; how could the cause be transmuted into the fruit? Therefore, ignorance is itself enlightenment.
The three thousand [realms] are both eternally identical in essence and identical in function.
Regarding "the three thousand are eternally so," "eternal" means there is no alteration; it is merely a change in phrasing. As for "essence and function":

since function pertains to the nine realms, it is said to be "function" due to delusion in the causal stage; since essence pertains to the Buddha-realm, it is said to be [the result] upon awakening in the fruition stage.
The former refers to cause as being identical to effect, while the latter refers to effect as being identical to cause; thus, cause and effect are non-dual.
This non-duality arises precisely because the three thousand realms all converge toward the principle (li).
Therefore, these two phrases establish non-duality within duality by virtue of the fact that the three thousand realms share the same principle of converging toward cause and effect.

Regarding the discussion of essence (*tǐ*) and function (*yòng*) within the ten realms (*daśadhātu*), the meanings do not follow a single path.

If one considers that all ten realms are provisional (*prajñapti*), then the Buddha-realm (*buddhadhātu*) also resides in function; this is as when both defilement and purity are entirely regarded as function.

If, however, one considers the nine realms to be provisional, then the Buddha-realm belongs to the essence; this is as stated in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-ṭīkā*: "Non-Dharma is function, while the Buddha-way is essence."
This essence is likewise so here; however, while the textual structure of the current passage and that of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* are identical, there are differences in their exegesis.
First, in that text, because there is no meaning that is not subsumed within what is accomplished, the three thousand realms belong to function and are termed "non-path";
thus, the essence of the Buddha-way is not said to be the three thousand realms. In the present text, the focus is on the point of return.
Because there is no realm that does not reach the ultimate meaning, the essence of the three thousand realms is such that its very substance is also called "the three thousand.

Second, in that [previous] text, the function is pointed out as being identical to the essence; in this text, the essence is pointed out as being identical to the function. Although both essence and function are present in both cases, many explanations differ.
The Correct Meaning (*Zhengyi*) states: "Delusion and enlightenment each have their own essence and function; within delusion, ignorance is taken as the essence."
The nine realms are manifested as function while taking the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) as their essence; the Buddha-realm is manifested as function. The *Wenxin* states:

"The three thousand [realms] are entirely the essence of the Dharma-body and the function of the two virtues. The *Yuantong* states: "The three thousand [realms] of cause and effect are both eternally abiding.
Since they are called "essence," they may also be called "function. The *Zhiyao* states: "The three [thousand realms] are inherently possessed within principle..."
The three thousand [realms] as cause are termed the "substance" (tǐ), and the three thousand [realms] as effect are termed the "function" (yòng).

Since the substance of the three thousand as cause and effect are both capable of giving rise to function—wherein the three thousand as cause give rise to defiled function and the three thousand as effect give rise to pure function—yet now it is said that all masters discuss substance and function separately based on the distinctness of cause and effect phenomena; however...

One may perceive that essence and function are non-dual, yet one has not yet seen that cause and effect are non-dual. Even if one were to say that since cause and effect each possess their own essence and function,
the essence and function of the cause are thus identical and non-dual with the essence and function of the fruit—

following the analogy of the *Jinbi* (The Golden Scalpel), which states that "though delusion and awakening differ, the substance of phenomena and principle is one"— if we examine this according to our current treatise, while the underlying intent may be consistent, it does not accord with the literal text.
In the preceding phrase, since the cause is pointed out as being identical to the fruit, the cause of ignorance is itself the fruit of awakened clarity.

Why, then, does the subsequent phrase discuss cause and fruit separately? It must be that the fruit is pointed out as being identical to the cause in order to accord with the essential nature of the text.

This is likely because [the author] was unaware of the function (*vṛtti*) inherent in the fruit; speaking in terms of its essential substance (*svabhāva*), this function belongs to the nine realms of existence, while the substance itself is the cause. However—

The commentary on the present text should clarify that both the essence and the function are the fruit, while both the essence and the function are the cause; because the fruit is pointed out as being identical to the cause, it is said that "both essence and function" are so designated.
Regarding the evaluation of the strengths and weaknesses of various masters' views, the meaning of the Correct Teaching (Shōgi) holds that the three thousand realms are solely essence;

the reason for speaking here of "function" is precisely because one points to function as being identical to the essence of the Dharma-nature, such that the entire essence of the three thousand realms constitutes this function.

If one employs only the "function" (yòng), then it is not the "three thousand" [realms]; this would be a mistake. If one employs both [body and function] together now, then the essential point is attained;
the mind-text is thus perfectly integrated. However, to take the "three thousand" as the function alone misses the mark. What is called "both" refers precisely to the three thousand.
If one points to the three thousand within emptiness as being without marks, how can one speak of "both"? This, too, captures the essential point.
Zhiwen’s *Pointing to the Essentials* states: "Because there is a distinction in the removal of ignorance, it is said that within the essence, the three thousand [realms] are perfectly manifest.

It further states: "In the perspective of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), it is called 'obscuration' because a single characteristic cannot be established; in the perspective of the provisional (*prajñapti*), it is called 'illumination' because the three thousand are perfectly manifest.
Why do these two formulations appear contradictory? Someone has answered: "The characteristics of sentient beings and phenomena are removed..."

Because ignorance has distinctions, within its very substance there are the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*); thus, the "one characteristic" (*ekalakṣaṇa*) cannot be established and the characteristics of deluded emotion (*sattvalakṣaṇa*) are extinguished.
One may now ask: when one employs provisional contemplation (*upāyadhyāna*), the three thousand [realms] are clearly manifested as they are;

is the characteristic of deluded emotion likewise extinguished? If you say it is not extinguished, how can the three thousand be revealed? If you say it is also extinguished, then even in provisional contemplation, the "one characteristic" would not be established.

Regarding the question of whether [the essence] exists, one should know that what the Four Clarities (Sì-míng) refers to as "distinctions within the essence" is based on the meaning of identity (*jì*).
This is truly because the *Zhǐyào* (Pointing to the Essentials) specifically addresses other schools who do not recognize the meaning of identity; thus, such a statement exists. Question:
Are these distinctions within the essence inherent evil (*xìng-è*) or cultivated evil (*xiū-è*)? Answer: The meaning now discussed applies to both the cultivated and the inherent; it follows from...
Evil, when taken as its very substance, is precisely cultivated evil; because cultivation-evil is identical to nature, it is precisely nature-evil.

Therefore, we know that those who speak of "possessing nature-evil" do so because cultivation is identical to nature, and thus they possess nature-evil. As for why the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) does not possess nature [in this sense], it is because it does not discuss identity;
thus, nature is not fully possessed. Since the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao) discusses identity, nature is fully possessed. This is...
When evil is discussed in terms of its nature (*svabhāva*), it can be said that if one does not speak of "immediacy" (*jì*), the meaning of "inclusion" (*yù*) cannot be established.
If evil is discussed in terms of its nature from the perspective of the Separate Teaching’s "Middle Only" (*biéjiào dànzhōng*), it cannot include evil;

since the nature of the "Middle Only" does not possess the nature of including evil, cultivated evil (*xiū'è*) cannot be immediately identical to that nature. In the Perfect Teaching (*yuánjiào*), on the contrary, it is precisely because of the nature of the "Perfect Middle" that [evil is included].

Because they possess the nature of evil, they cultivate evil; yet, being able to realize that this very [cultivation] is the nature itself, it may also be said that if one does not speak of "possession" (*ju*), the meaning is not established.
Although these two meanings differ, their essential intent is no different.

Furthermore, one must understand that within the pedagogical gate of the One Vehicle, regarding the provisional dharmas of the nine realms, the characteristics and substance of sentient beings, and the three types of emotion, each of the nine realms is individually [identical].
There is a state of deluded attachment wherein the characteristics of the nine realms are taken as distinct entities; thus, there appear to be two aspects to their essence:
first, when the essence is distinguished according to its characteristics, there is the essence of the nine realms' differentiation;

second, when the essence is discussed in terms of its ultimate reality, the differentiation of the nine realms possesses only its characteristics and lacks any inherent self-nature, for all are identical in being the one single nature that constitutes the nine realms.
