The three types of retinues perceive the "convenient" [land] within the "true reward" [land], and they likewise perceive their own bodies.
If one reconciles the present passage with the previous statement that the single nature is inherently endowed with both self and other, it encompasses two meanings:

first, the preceding text speaks generally of being endowed with both self and other, whereas the present text specifically mentions the single nature being endowed with the other; thus, in a single thought-moment, there is quiescence.

Light is precisely that which is of the single nature of equality. Second, within the aforementioned two types of "possessors," it is in reference to emptiness and space that they function as possessors;
this is what is meant in the present text by the "land of the tranquil radiant light" (*sukhāvatī*) being the "functioning application.

Since this functioning application is that which is possessed, it does not depart from emptiness and space. Therefore, it is said that it does not go beyond its essence; since the essence and the application are identical, [the two are one].

The non-duality of self and other is precisely the equality of the single nature; when this essence is realized as emptiness, the meanings of "extinction" (亡) and "illumination" (照) are unified to form the principle of essence and function.
Taking this essence as "self" in contrast to the transformative function of "other," we establish the gates of self and other;

the subsequent sections on the mirror and clarity all share this same intent. △ Second, showing how the three thousand [realms] are possessed, such that the capacity and response accord with the Way. Part One.
Regarding the two aspects of the Dharma, the first shows the fundamental cause of the stimulus and response:

because sentient beings inherently possess the three thousand [realms] within their principle, they are able to stimulate the Buddhas; because the three thousand realms are fully perfected within the principle, the Buddhas are able to respond.
The principle is as stated in the preceding text: "a single thought-moment of the serene light" (*jìguāng*) may refer either to emptiness (*kōng*) or to equality (*píngděng*).

Because it exists in fruition (*guǒ*), it is "fulfilled" (*mǎn*); because it exists within delusion (*mí*), it is "complete" (*jù*). This completeness and this fulfillment are one and the same three thousand worlds (*sānqiān*). It is only through the Buddha’s arising that there can be a response;

it is only through the existence of beings that there can be an invocation. What is now being expounded is the non-duality of self and other; it does not mean that there is merely a single set of three thousand worlds.
To discuss non-duality through the three thousand [realms] means simply to take the three thousand as the "other" (the response), for within the emptiness of one's own practice, they are non-dual.
If one were to directly treat the three thousand as the non-duality of self and other, one would not yet have seen the non-duality of self and other;
for although sentient beings possess the principle (*li*), since it has not yet been manifested, they lack the virtues realized through their own practice. Since the Buddha...

Because the fulfillment of principle (*ri-man*) is that which one has personally realized through one's own practice, it benefits others precisely through that self-practice; thus, the fulfillment of principle is what constitutes the capacity to respond.

For this reason, in the text, the "three thousand" are placed under "principle-endowment" (*ri-gu*) with respect to the sentient beings (*ki*), while the "fulfillment of principle" is placed under "three thousand" with respect to the responsive capacity (*ōng*).
There is profound significance in this. Therefore, although the three [thousand worlds] are mentioned from the perspective of the Buddha, [the distinction remains].

The "thousand" refers to taking the three thousand realms within emptiness as the "capable responder" (*nengying*). Regarding the side of birth-and-death, although it is said that the principle is complete therein, one takes the three thousand realms of good and evil as the "capable evoker" (*nengganshen*).

That the three thousand realms within emptiness are the self is the "evoked" (*sugan*), while the three thousand realms of the other are the "evoker" (*tagan*. This is the purport of non-duality in this present text. If not... [text fragment ends].

How, then, can this unify the preceding and following passages? Furthermore, the preceding text states, "From benefiting oneself, one benefits others," while the subsequent text states, "The non-arising of self-nature is without spatial location. △ Second, showing the convergence of the path of response and resonance.
It should be that the response is universally and joyfully directed toward every capacity without error.

Because the response is universal with respect to every capacity, and every capacity is universally joyful toward the response, it follows that the response is directed accordingly; thus, the resonance between stimulus and response is without error.
If one asks how both the capacity and the response can be without error when they are both comprised within the Three Thousand [Realms], the answer is that in this text, there is no error.
One must encompass two meanings: first, if one discusses the "other" (the object) alone, there are three thousand [phenomena] in the response and three thousand in the stimulus;

this may also be called the non-differentiation of stimulus and response. However, within the response, it is specifically the function of the response being identical to that of sentient beings which constitutes non-differentiation.
Therefore, it is said: "The three thousand [phenomena] for transforming others respond to things; that which can respond and that which can transform are [identical]."

That which is to be responded to and that which is to be transformed constitute the "capacity" (the *ki*); therefore, this subject and object are without distinction, both being subsumed under the character "other" (*ta*).
Second, when discussing self and other together: the single character "self" (*ji*) is also the "responder" (*ōō*).

From the perspective of the responder, the essence of the responder—being empty—is taken as "self," while in contrast to the "other" who is to be transformed, it is called "self and other. Thus, it is said: "self and other."
Second, it is precisely because the principle of the emptiness of the three thousand worlds has already been fully revealed that one should naturally respond without error.
△ Second, the analogy, which has three parts: first, the proposition.
Otherwise, how could it manifest images like a mirror?

If it is not admitted that because the three thousand worlds are complete according to principle, the capacity of the sentient beings and the response of the Buddha do not miss one another, how could it be like an image appearing in a mirror?
Now, I am not saying that for an image to appear there must necessarily be a form; nor am I saying that for a mirror to exist there must necessarily be a form facing it.
However, if the analogy of the mirror were not clear, then the principle of the Dharma would be obscured.
Regarding this, I shall briefly explain it now. The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra* states: "Because it illuminates the Middle, it is a mirror; because it illuminates the True (zhen), it is purity;

because it illuminates the Conventional (su), it is clarity. Because it is clear, the image is manifest; because it is pure, flaws are exhausted and the True is revealed; because it is a mirror, the substance is perfect and the Middle is revealed.
Zhiyi [Zhang’an] takes the aspect of clarity’s ability to manifest images as the conventional, and thus regards clarity as the conventional. If...
In the *Zhiguan*, the mirror is used as a metaphor for the Middle Way (*madhyamā*), the clarity of the mirror for emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and the images for the provisional (*prajñapti*).

In the *Miaojiji*, the clarity of the mirror’s nature is used to illustrate the cultivation of the ten suchnesses; here, clarity is used to illustrate emptiness, the images to illustrate the provisional, and the roundness of the mirror to illustrate the Middle.
Alternatively, one may use the clarity to illustrate emptiness, the images to illustrate the provisional, and the roundness of the mirror to illustrate the level.

Regarding "the nature of the ten realms is identical to the single nature": the two characters for "ten realms" represent that which is possessed, while the single character for "nature" represents the possessor;
thus, they are identical to the "mirror" and the "image. Now, this passage also encompasses these two meanings:
first, the mirror metaphor signifies equality, which is the fundamental [nature], while the image in the sky metaphor signifies the single nature manifesting in response to objects.
Other mirrors must necessarily possess luminosity; the subsequent statement that "it is obscured by dust" implicitly contains the meaning of luminosity.

Second, since the mirror and its luminosity are identical, they both serve as metaphors for the image within space, which in turn serves as a metaphor for conventional cognition (*prajñapti*). Having understood this point, one may then discuss the Dharma.
△ Second, the explanation of the three [aspects]. First, the sequential explanation:
A mirror possesses the principle (*li*) of manifesting images; a form possesses the nature (*xing*) of producing images.
"Principle" refers to the underlying logic (*taoli*); "nature" refers to the essential constituent (*xingfen*). Question: What do "principle" and "nature" metaphorically represent? Answer: First—
Only after clarifying the principle of the dharma of resonance (ganying) may one then explain the parables. This consists of two parts: a general discussion and a specific discussion.
Each of these contains two meanings. Regarding the two meanings of the general discussion: first, a general clarification of the capacity (ji) and the response (ying);

second, the principle that this capacity and response pervades both emptiness (kong) and phenomena (shi), as well as the three thousand [realms]. The text states: "The principle (li) [pervades] the capacity within emptiness," and it is fully endowed with the three thousand [realms].

Therefore, it is able to evoke the principle of the three thousand [worlds] (which corresponds to the "emptiness" [of the response]), and because it is fulfilled, it is able to respond. To discuss this separately:

first, regarding the distinctiveness of the capacity to respond, as the preceding text states, "benefiting others according to their capacities," and as it says later, "only then can one establish myriad phenomena in accordance with the nature, responding without fixed location," and so forth.
Second, the response is distinct within emptiness, while the capacities [of beings] are distinct within the three thousand. Furthermore...
How can this application arise? Is it not because the Buddha himself has personally realized emptiness?
Although there exists the principle of emptiness within the capacity of the sentient beings, they do not take emptiness as the cause for their invocation;
rather, they take the phenomena of the three thousandfold world. This is because the essence of the principle of emptiness is present in all things.

Therefore, there are those who do not move the Buddha because they have not yet engaged in the matters that can move him; this is because sentient beings manifest good and evil within their activities, and thus the capacity to move him resides specifically in the cultivation of such activities. Question: Since the principle inherently possesses the three thousand [realms], it is capable of moving [the Buddha];

however, how can the inherent possession of the three thousand within the principle be considered the cultivation of activities? Answer: The principle within emptiness is that which is capable [of moving the Buddha].

The three thousand mundane phenomena are that which is possessed; yet this possession, if it were identical to the act of possessing, would mean that the act of creating is itself a mundane phenomenon.
Therefore, when considering the capacity to evoke the Buddha, whether one performs good or evil deeds constitutes the practice of phenomena.

These practices of phenomena are entirely the three thousand [phenomena]; they are in reality no different from the functional activity of the Buddha-fruit, differing only in being the substance within emptiness.

Because the nature is deluded and has not yet manifested, the wondrous function of the three thousand [realms] likewise has not yet been revealed; this is what is referred to as "inherent in principle" (*liju*).
If one were to claim that the capacity to respond does not exist apart from the cultivated phenomena (*xiushi*), then why would all sentient beings be unable to respond?

It is because the substance within this emptiness (*kongzhong*) has not yet manifested. If the substance has not manifested, there is no means by which it can respond to objects. As it is said: [text fragment].

It is said that while the Three Thousandfold World has not yet been manifested and verified, its substance remains obscure; because the substance is manifested, the function of the Three Thousandfold World is revealed.
In this text, "self" and "other" correctly refer to the self that is capable of responding and the other that is capable of evoking; both are naturally inherent within the fundamental nature.
When the Tathāgata realizes this, his own realization immediately benefits others; thus, the non-duality of self and other is established from this point onward. If one follows...
The illustrative analogy is also distinct; as for the mirror analogy employed here, it is intended to illustrate how this response arises.
Thus, the mirror represents the substance within space, while the physical form represents the responsive capacity that evokes it.

Although the image is used to represent the response, this is merely to clarify that the causal power to produce the image resides in the mirror; therefore, the mirror is said to possess the manifestation.
The principle of the image is illustrated by its capacity to respond within the substance of space.
If there were only the substance of the mirror and no formal phenomena, from what would the image arise? Although it is the formal phenomenon that arises, space serves as its substance.

Space is a metaphor for the inherent principle (*li*), while form is a metaphor for the three thousand [realms]. The response of the image occurs within the form and not within space; therefore, form possesses arising.
Regarding the nature of the image, it is stated below that "form and activity are themselves the nature. This does not mean that phenomena (dharma) are not perceived;

rather, it is merely a matter of speaking in terms of "phenomena" or "principle" (li). Question: Why is it said that form takes emptiness as its substance? Answer: Here we speak from the perspective of phenomena.
Since an image appears by depending upon the brightness of a mirror, it takes the brightness of the mirror as the substance of the image. Form, however, arises from empty space.
Because it stands [upon something], it grasps empty space to form its physical body; thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Due to delusive ignorance there is empty space;

depending on space, the world is established. Generally speaking, both the environment (*āśraya*) and its inhabitants (*adhiṣṭhāna*) are termed the "world" (*loka*). △ Second, the inverse explanation.
If a single form could not manifest its image,
then by the very fact that it *cannot* manifest [other things], it is revealed that it *can* manifest;
thus, the principle of the mirror would be exhausted.
If a mirror cannot manifest images, it would mean that the principle of the mirror is exhausted; this serves as a metaphor for the substance within emptiness (*ākāśa*).
If that substance within emptiness cannot give rise to a response, it implies that the substance of emptiness has reached its limit.

The intended meaning is that if emptiness could only give rise to a response toward this particular capacity (*indriya*) and could not give rise to a response toward that capacity, then [it would be limited].
The substance within space is finite, and that which can serve as its metaphor is likewise so; therefore, it is said to be "a single form.

Since the form and the matter do not interpenetrate, when a form and a matter face a mirror, there must be a reflection; yet if a form faces a mirror, it cannot produce a manifested image of the matter.

There is no such principle [that would allow for this]. "Tong" (通) is synonymous with "dao" (道). This metaphor implies that the "ji" (機, the stimulus/response mechanism) must be able to evoke a "ying" (應, the response).

If the mechanism does not evoke a response, then the function of the mechanism will be obstructed. Previously, the principle of the mirror was used as a metaphor for the essential nature of emptiness;
now, the worldly affairs of form are used as a metaphor for the affairs of the stimulus and response. △ Third, the dual explanation by reversing and following [the sequence].
Regarding the first form, the first part provides a counter-interpretation:
If it were possible for the form and the mirror to be separated, such a principle might exist;

likewise, if it were possible for the capacity (the sentient being) and the response (the Buddha) to be separated, such a principle might exist. By means of this text, it is made clear that our current explanation is correct, as the form [is not separated].
Regarding the analogy of the reflected image and the separation between the stimulus and the response: is that which responds the image or the mirror?
If one says it is the mirror, then the mirror serves as the analogy for empty space to clarify the present meaning, which accords with the intent of this text.

If one says it is the image, then according to the current text, it should have stated that "the form and the image are separated," yet it only mentions the mirror; is this not intended to specifically take empty space as the responding agent?
It should be so heard. △ Second, the sequential explanation:
"There is no form that faces it and is not reflected.
The character for "mirror" is omitted, as its meaning is already evident from the preceding text. △ Second, the mirror [has two parts]: first, the refutation.

If it is argued that the mirror does not manifest images because they are obstructed by dust, and that the essence [of consciousness] has not yet arisen because it is covered by afflictions (*kleśa*), this statement should apply only to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and not to those with spiritual capacity (*yogin*).
Furthermore, if you say the essence has not yet arisen, you must explain why the mirror does not manifest images; is this not a matter pertaining to the image itself?
Question: Why was the mirror used as the analogy for the response? Answer: To clarify this meaning, we shall now explain it through two pairs of "agent" (neng) and "object" (suo).
First, the mirror is the agent and the image is that which is produced by the agent.

Second, if one considers the mirror and the image in relation to the sentient capacity (ji), the mirror is the agent of response and the capacity is the object of response; within the context of the agent of response, space is the agent.

The substance that responds is the mundane phenomenon, while the function of responding is its activity. When distinguishing between self and other, one must take the substance that responds as the "self";

therefore, one does not take the function of responding as the self. In the preceding passage, where it was said that the form and the mirror are separated, this precisely refers to the substance that responds;
thus, the mirror is taken as the "responding" entity. In the present passage, however, the mirror has not yet appeared.
As for "images," they are taken because they serve as responsive applications; thus, one takes images to be the responsive.
One should know that if the principles of the Dharma are correct, there will be little doubt or obstruction among various explanations. △ Second, the Conforming [Section].
The removal of dust depends on the person who polishes; the manifestation of the image does not depend on the polisher.

Dust is a metaphor for delusion, the person is a metaphor for the practitioner cultivating contemplation on the causal stage, and polishing is a metaphor for the practitioner’s cultivation of contemplation to destroy delusions and manifest emptiness.
What would be inappropriate about this? Furthermore, the fact that this emptiness can give rise to functional application is entirely... [the result].
The original existence is not obtained through cultivation. △ Third, the synthesis.
By observing the Dharma through analogies, the general principle can be understood.
△ Third, explaining that what is inherently possessed is manifested through cultivation. Part one: restating the preceding point.

One should know that although the principle is fully possessed by both self and other, nevertheless, within this single nature, both self and other are fully present. △ Second, showing the cultivation [of the two]: first, attaining the fruit through the cause;
second, first cultivating the arousal [of the mind] to transform others.
It must rely on the conditions of the "enlightened cause" (pariniṣpanna-hetu), which serves as the causal basis for the merit of benefiting others.
The principle of "fruition through mastery" (k-ka) inherently possesses both self and other, which constitutes the three truths.

Now, when the two types of cultivation—conditional (en) and causal (ryo)—are combined with the nature (shō) of these three to form the Middle Way, the conditional and causal aspects are taken as the merit of benefiting others. Furthermore, regarding the inherent possession of self and other within the principle, the "other" manifested through cultivation is first clarified;
this refers to the two kinds of conditional and causal factors: wisdom and practice, as well as the primary and auxiliary conditions.

That is to say, conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) also serves as the object-condition for correct wisdom; it assists in the practice that severs the dust-like delusions and reveals the principle of conventional truth.
△ Second, the cultivation and arousal of one’s own practice. This, in turn, proceeds by means of the object-condition and the contributing condition.
By means of the cause, it unites with the nature;
by means of the fruition, it brings about the result. This is the condition of merit through the definitive eradication of the delusions of ignorance by means of the Middle Way and right wisdom.

To assist in manifesting the Middle Way of True Emptiness, it is said by way of analogy that they are "unified as one": the cultivation of the conditions and the understanding merges with the nature of reality until they are indistinguishably one.

This refers to the unification of nature and function when considering the merit of benefiting others, spanning from the stages prior to the [ten] abodes through the causal stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyag-avakrānti-bhūmi*) up to the ultimate fruit.
△ Second, showing the characteristics of the realization of the fruit, in two parts: first, the demonstration.
Only then can one, in accordance with the nature (*dharmatā*), establish the myriad phenomena;
by conforming to the essence within emptiness, one gives rise to the three thousand transformative functions. △ Second, the explanation:
thus, if the self-nature does not arise, there would be no spatial location.
Because it moves in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), it does not give rise to conceptual constructs; because it is universal, it has no spatial or temporal origin.

It reveals that the self and others are inherently complete together, and that the self immediately benefits others; now, this is manifested as identical to the aforementioned attainment of the fruit.

Since the self immediately benefits others, is this not the non-duality of self and other? Is it not the practice for oneself within emptiness while simultaneously transforming others? This is what is called "perfect penetration" in the preceding text.

Originally, the inherent nature of self and other, as well as the benefit of others through the very act of benefiting oneself, all reside within the realm of function. Yet, in the commentary on the current passage, it instead states:

"If one does not give rise to the practice of self-benefit, the nature within emptiness is inherently endowed with the three thousand inconceivable provisional phenomena; only then can one respond universally to beings without being restricted by location.
Now I say: this explanation is a misunderstanding of the text. If, as it says here, one does not give rise to the self-nature, then [the capacity for response] would be non-existent.
How does this "place" differ from what was previously stated regarding the identity of benefiting oneself and others?

Furthermore, if one establishes the categories of self and other solely based on the capacity of the transformative agent and the object of transformation—without referring to emptiness as being "other"—then I do not yet understand where one might perceive the non-duality of one's own practice and the transformation of others.
One should know that these [distinctions] are merely established conventionally within the subsequent five wondrous stages.

Regarding the six gates, their defilement and purity, their reliance on the primary and secondary [realms], and their three karmas—whether provisional or real—all are established according to the responsive manifestation;
they belong to the capacity of those who receive moisture, yet none of them clarify the non-duality of one's own practice versus the transformation of others.

Therefore, the gate of "self and other" is placed in the midst of the six gates to penetrate both above and below; through this, one sees that self and other are of one essence and non-dual. Without this, [the teaching remains incomplete].
The gates merely show that within the ten gates, one’s own practice and the transformation of others each clarify non-duality. △ Third, the conclusion:
This is established by the gate of the non-duality of the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya* and *adhiṣṭhāna*).

That which manifests as the environment and inhabitants on the level of fruition is the entire body [of reality]; the preceding [discussion] concerned only the function of the environment and inhabitants.

Because it is argued that there is no difference in the essence of the responsive capacity and because it is discussed as non-dual, the "Gate of Self and Other" is established based on the distinction between the environment and its inhabitants. △ First, the heading:
The Eighth Gate, "The Non-duality of the Three Karmas."

The essence of this gate of non-duality is sometimes expressed through emptiness (*śūnyatā*) or sometimes pointed to as the single nature (*ekasvabhāva*). The *Wenxin* states: "The body wheel (*kāyacakram*) fundamentally belongs to the preceding gate;
this gate properly pertains to the secret of speech (*vāgmudrā*). This text clarifies the perfect penetration and practical application by showing how these three are interrelated.
Following the intent of the *Wenxin*, it says: "Although the teaching belongs to the mouth, could there not be the body and mind? Thus, the body wheel [is also involved]."
Although this belongs to the preceding [section on] supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), what harm is there in clarifying it concurrently?

Now, if one says it is not so, how could the distinctness of oral secrecy (*vāg-guhyaka*) be explained if it were not uniquely non-dual? As for the statement that this gate is established from the perspective of preaching the Dharma:

although the pure function of the gate of defilement and purity (*saṃkleśa-vyavadāna*) pervades all three karmas, its specific locus is in the mind. This is because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) serves as...
Because it is used for purification, although its basis—the gate of the primary and secondary [recompenses]—pervades all three karmas, it specifically resides in the body.
Therefore, the text says: "the superior and inferior bodies. Now, in this gate of the three karmas, they actually pervade all three;

however, in contrast to the previous specific [treatment], they are provisionally said to reside specifically in speech. Thus, it simply says they are established from "preaching the Dharma. If one were to discern their non-duality...
The "combined clarification of the three karmas" does not mean that they arrive by being mutually associated or mutually established. Why is this?

Because in the preceding sections on the two gates of the environment and the sentient beings, and of defilement and purity, one merely used the environment to contrast with the sentient beings and defilement to contrast with purity to explain non-duality;

one had never yet explained the non-duality of the three karmas within the primary retribution (*vipāka*) and within the pure functions. Therefore, the present passage should be understood as treating these three [karmas] individually.

Because the faculty of hearing is clarified, the non-dual essence encompasses both directions and unifies them as one. First, within emptiness, because emptiness itself constitutes the response to the three karmas, they are non-dual.
Second, their single nature is established because the True Body (dharmakāya) likewise manifests the three karmas;
when the True Body speaks of reality, this is speech, which necessarily implies the mental wheel (*manas-cakra*). Thus, they are of a single nature, fused within the Truth.
Question: Since the two kinds of threefold action (trikarma) are both non-dual, how can there be threefold action in the True Body (*dharmakāya*), which is without marks (*animitta*)?

Answer: From the perspective of the essential nature of the Dharma (*dharmatā*), there are no threefold actions; however, now, in accordance with its functional application, this True Body is also described as having threefold action.

Furthermore, although it has no separate substance, it is provisionally designated by names in accordance with the world; therefore, it is ultimately characterized by the equality of the single nature (*ekalakṣaṇa*). It is not [merely] that there is no [threefold action].
The essence of "name" is fused; in this True Body, the three karmas are non-dual. If one asks what is meant by "non-dual," it must be contrasted with the duality of the three karmas.
What is the meaning of this? The answer is: First, all distinctions whatsoever are termed "dual," and the distinction between the three karmas likewise belongs to the dual.
As in the following [passage], receiving the intercalary month brings tenfold benefits; because of these differences...

Because they are distinct, they are also called "two," though this does not necessarily refer to two directions as being "two. Since the preceding various differences all constitute two dharmas, they are merely differentiated by means of "two.
Although there are ten types of reception of the intercalary month (*rūn*), they only result in the benefit of the two kinds:
the provisional and the real. The three karmas of the present are precisely the two of form and mind; therefore, the text below states:

Form and mind are of one suchness. △ Second, the explanation [of the title] has two parts: first, showing the three secrets of the fruit-Buddha; second, clarifying that there is no difference between the mind and the Buddha.

Since all ten gates are established for the purpose of contemplation (*guan*), they synthesize the causes and fruits of one’s own practice as well as the capacities and objects of transforming others into contemplation.
Therefore, it is necessary to name each according to its own fundamental dharma without hindrance to discussing other Buddhas.

The realization of the fruit is the dharma-gate of my ordinary mind; regarding what is taught in this passage—that the mind and the Buddha are without difference—although the wording appears later, the essential meaning actually lies at the beginning.
Furthermore, within the gates of self and other, although it is said that [the nature] is manifested through cultivation, this refers to the person who has attained the fruit;
therefore, it says "only then can one... and so forth, including "not giving rise to [delusions]" and the like. If one were to debate based solely on the literal text, it would seem as though...

Throughout the beginning and end of this single gate, the "contemplation of mind" has not yet been seen; it is only now that we encounter it. One should know that since the meaning of the text is established as the contemplation of mind, then self and others are not separate from the present moment of thought.
There is no need for further discrimination, for its essential principle is already clear. This initial section is further divided into two parts:

first, directly clarifying the function of the fruit; second, [the sub-section] showing the three mysteries. Within the first of these, there is a general clarification of the three mysteries; within that, the first part shows them.

Regarding the three secrets (*triguhya*), there are two aspects: their names and their essential nature (*svabhāva*). First, concerning the essential nature: within the context of benefiting others, the three secrets are categorized as "phenomenal" (*dharma*) because they are derived from the *nirmāṇakāya* (the body of transformation).

Although these three secrets are essentially derived from the *saṃbhogakāya* (the enjoyment body), they are designated as "phenomenal" with respect to the ultimate principle-body (*dharmatākāya*). This is as stated in the *Myōki* (Wondrous Record).

It is said that whenever one speaks of the "three mysteries," it must necessarily refer to the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya), the self-enjoyment body (svasaṃbhogakāya), the reward body (saṃbhogakāya), and the equal dharma-body (samatā-dharmakāya);
regarding these, what could possibly be called "mysterious"? △ Second, the names:
they are named differently according to how they accord with the nature of phenomena.
First, the Dharma-body is not three, yet it manifests as three according to the capacities of sentient beings; thus, the names differ.
Second, regarding the three karmas realized by the Tathāgata, they are mutually fused; the designations "body, speech, and mind" differ only to accord with sentient beings.
Third, it is simply body, speech, and mind that are termed the three karmas, the three secrets, the three wheels, the three non-guardings, the three absences of error, and so forth.
All these are merely in accordance with phenomena; the four *siddhāntas* respond to capacities according to the principles of things.
When the principles accorded to the capacities of beings can be termed different from those of ordinary people, they are called "secret," "wheel," "unprotected," or "without fault.
Alternatively, when the principles accorded to the capacities of beings can be termed the same, the body, speech, and mind are likewise called "karma."
I have previously argued that the Buddha’s arising in response is identical to the activities performed by sentient beings; however, others raise this objection:
"How can the Buddha's three mysteries (sanmitsu) be termed 'activity' (gyō)? This is merely a lapse in memory on their part.

Now, the reason they are designated as "three activities" (sangyō) in the *Fumon* [The Gate of Non-duality] and given the name "activity" is that the performance of a task is what is termed "activity. Furthermore, regarding what the Buddha performs within the present text:
The body manifests supernatural powers, the mouth expounds the Dharma, and the mind discerns the capacities of sentient beings—these constitute his activities.

If he responds universally to the six realms of existence by employing the means of "harmony through shared activity" (*samānārthatā*), it appears identical to the activities performed by ordinary beings;

yet, within the Buddha’s wondrous realization, these must be entirely the essence itself. Since there is nothing that is produced, what activity could there be? It is merely a provisional designation in accordance with the capacities of beings.

Regarding the term "karma," there are two ways to understand the names of the three types of karma: first, they generally encompass both cause and effect; second, they are specifically restricted to the causal stage.
Therefore, in the *Myōku* (Exquisite Verses), the three karmas of the "Peaceful and Blissful Practice" (*Anrakugyō*) are explained as being in the causal stage.

If one speaks of the "three secrets" (*sanmitsu*) or the "three wheels" (*sarin*), these pertain exclusively to the resultant stage. As the *Jōmyōki* states: "Within each of the realms, each possesses ten [aspects]," and thus one must not [confuse them].

Because one realm cannot be measured by means of many realms, it is called "mysterious" (*guhya*). The *Maha-yan-ming-lun* (Great Mysterious Treatise) states: "The Buddha has three mysteries that all humans and devas cannot comprehend or know.
Question: What is meant by "mystery"? Is it the truth (*satya*) or is it concealment (*gupti*)? Answer: From the perspective of the ultimate intention (*tāttvika-artha*), it is the truth;

from the perspective of phenomenal application (*prayoga*), it is the very essence (*svabhāva*). Since each realm possesses ten [attributes] and the whole essence functions as application, there is no application that is not [the essence].

Because Sōe (Saichō) was devoted to the teachings of Kannon, the Esoteric Texts (*Hiken*) specifically speak of the "Three Mysteries" (*sanmitsu*) and "Four Gates" (*shimon*). To cause others not to know through the power of the inconceivable is precisely what is meant by "hidden" (*inmitsu*). Question: If the "thoroughly penetrating mystery" (*tsūshinmitsu*) belongs to the Dharma-body (*hosshin*), then how can the *Myōki* (the *Shugo Kokkai Shō*) refer to it as the "Equal Dharma-body" (*byōdō hosshin*) while discussing what is "mysterious"? Answer: It is explained in terms of the three [bodies] (*sansoku*). Specifically, the "Equal Dharma-body" refers to the Reward-body (*hōshin*), which is the "mystery of the body" (*shinmitsu*). Furthermore, because the "inconceivable mystery" (*fushigimitsu*) is the mystery of the mind (*shinmitsu*), and the "thoroughly penetrating mystery" is the mystery of speech (*gomitsu*), these three mysteries are collectively referred to as the "Equal Dharma-body. Thus, it is said that the Equal Dharma-body is the "mystery of the body," and the inconceivable mystery is the "mystery of the mind. Therefore, the three mysteries are established based on the three bodies. Consequently, the "thoroughly penetrating mystery" is the mystery of speech, and the "equal mystery" is the mystery of the mind; thus, the three mysteries are established based on the three bodies. This is why the *Myōki* states: "The equal Dharma-body is the mystery of the body. Because the secret [nature] resides in the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), it is precisely due to the fact that the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) does not distinguish among the three;

now, because the true secret resides within the application [of the response-body], they are called the "three secrets. △ Second, showing that the three wheels accord with sentient beings without error.
The Mind-Wheel (citta-cakra) discerns capacities, while the two wheels [of body and speech] establish transformation and manifest the Dharma; there has never been even a hair’s breadth of error.

The Buddha’s body, speech, and mind are a single entity without distinction; yet, proceeding from their functional differentiation, because the Mind discerns capacities, it causes the two wheels to establish transformation without fail.
Because these two are able to grind away the defilements of sentient beings, they are called "wheels" (*cakra*). Question: Regarding the Buddha’s mind...
If it is necessarily the Middle Way and the Dharma-nature, why then do you say that the Dharmakāya is not secret? Answer: If the entire body is taken as the mind, then it is the Middle Way;

however, if one speaks only in terms of its essential nature (*dharmatā*), it is not called "mind. When contrasted with the functions of body and speech, the mind is established as the "mind" (*citta*).
If one speaks directly in terms of function, all the various minds of the Buddha are ultimately nothing but compassion; this mind exists entirely as such.
Question: When the mind arises as the mind, does the "mind-wheel" that examines the capacity of the faculty constitute *manasikāra* (mental attention) or not?

Answer: Because it pertains to the actual function of the essence, it belongs to *manasikāra*. This is truly because the Tathāgata provisionally manifests the dharma of the mind; therefore, he engaged in reflection for twenty-one days regarding this matter.
If it were not *manasikāra*, how could it be called "reflection"? It is also as stated in the "Universal Gate Chapter": [the Bodhisattva] dwells in the practice of the six perfections, etc.

That which is relied upon for the application of "should" is precisely the nature of equality; what thought or action could there be? It is like an image appearing in a mirror—does the mirror have a mind?
Therefore, in the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), it is stated that the Buddha’s "mental attention" (*manasikāra*) is a refutation of the views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
There are two kinds of manifesting supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*): first, the places where the Tathāgata manifests his body are themselves supernatural powers; second, there is actual manifestation.

The "Constant Body" (nityakāya) manifests supernormal powers (ṛddhi), while the "Dharma-flower Radiance Body" (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-prabhā-kāya) refers to the manifestation of supernormal powers without yet emitting this radiance.

This is the Constant Body which merely preaches the Dharma or attains liberation through silence; silence itself is also considered preaching. △ Second, specifically clarifying the two [aspects of] body and speech.
First, the establishment [of the categories].
Regarding the distinction between the Body and the Dharma, there is the distinction between the Real and the Provisional, and the distinction between the Expedient and the Real.

This twofold division is established by contrasting the partial and the perfect: from the perspective of the Body, one distinguishes the Real and the Responsive; from the perspective of the Dharma, one distinguishes the Expedient and the Real.

Because within the Perfect Teaching the Responsive is understood to be identical to the Dharma, it is termed the "Real Body" (*dharmakāya*); though it is called the "Real Body," it is in fact the Responsive.
For example, the Contemplation Sūtra’s “Contemplation of the True Dharmakāya” refers to the *saṃbhogakāya* as the "True Dharma" (zhēn fǎ).

Synthesizing various texts, the name "Dharmakāya" (fǎshēn) contains two meanings for the character "dharma" (*fǎ*): first, the dharma of principle (*lǐfǎ*), and second, the dharma of wisdom (*zhìfǎ*).
Because [the Buddha] employs these dharmas, all three bodies are called the Dharmakāya. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-śāstra* states: "The true, pure dharma of Vairocana Buddha..."

Regarding the two—the Dharmakāya of Vairocana Buddha, which is pure and perfected, and the Nirmāṇakāya of Śākyamuni Buddha, which is a responsive transformation—these two "dharmas" are in fact the principle-dharma (*dharmatā*).
Depending on the context, it receives various names, yet they do not exceed three types: first, the principle-Dharmakāya; second, the Dharmakāya within its activity (the *svabhāvikakāya*);
and third, the body that has attained the dharma (the *dharmakāya* as realization), as described in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* as the "Buddha of the Dharma-nature Body."

Regarding these four masters, when they had not yet attained the Way, they were called "birth-bodies" (*janmakāya*); because they had already attained the Way, they were called "dharma-bodies" (*dharmakāya*). An ancient said:
"The dharma-body within its function is not the same as the principle-substance (*tattva*). Shenzhi further said: "The body that has attained the Dharma is also not the same as the substance.
Now, it is said that following the literal sense of the term "Dharma," the character "Dharma" is identical; it functions according to what it signifies.
Because they are distinguished, there is the "Dharmatā-body Buddha" (dharma-nature body), which is established by virtue of attaining the *dharmatā* within enlightenment;
it is also called the "body that has attained the Dharma" because it likewise realizes and attains the *dharmatā*. One must not lose sight of their single essence by following these designations.

When it is spoken of in terms of its functional manifestation, it is called the "Dharmakāya in function"; when it is spoken of in terms of its realization and attainment, it is called the "body that has attained the Dharma. Regarding the Dharma...
Each single character is the essence of principle (*dharmatā*). Question: Since both "Reality" (*tattva*) and "Dharmatā" are employed [as synonyms], are the two bodies (*kāya*) identical?

Answer: In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Dharmatā extends throughout both the Real Reward Land (*sambhogakāya-bhūmi*) and the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-kṣetra*), as well as the partial teachings (*pradeśa-dharma*).
△ Second, the explanation of the two [bodies]: the first two bodies and their two explanations cannot be different.

If the two bodies were different, why would it be said that they are "identical to the Dharma-body"? If these two explanations were contradictory, why would it be said that "all attain the Buddha-way"?
To point to the Response-body as being the Dharma-body is to follow the [Lotus] land; to point to the Buddha of the Tripiṭaka as being the Perfect True Body is to follow the teaching.
This refers to the fact that the Response Body (nirmāṇakāya) of the Perfectly Victorious One is indeed the True Body;

or it refers to the Response Bodies of the three teachings being identical to the True [Body], such that all attain the Buddha-way. It refers to the provisional as being identical to the real, whereby the spoken Dharma reveals the speaking mouth:
the mouth that speaks the provisional is itself the real mouth. △ Second, the two bodies and two modes of teaching cannot be one.
If there were only the Dharma-body, it would not descend into the world.
If there were only the Dharma-body of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), there would be no descent into the world of the response-bodies (ying-shen) of the three teachings.
If there were only the Buddha-way, who would bestow the three vehicles?

It is said that the Buddha-way of the Three Vehicles is also manifested by means of what it can reveal. If there were only the mouth that speaks of the Buddha-way, who would then discourse upon the provisional application of the Dharma?
One cannot argue that the former case is different from the opening of the provisional, nor can one argue that the latter case is identical to the application of the provisional.

This is simply because one wishes to distinguish whether the Buddha’s body and speech are one or different; it should not be difficult to claim that what was opened previously is the same as what is applied later.

Giving may also be opened up to provide further opportunities for those whose capacities require it. △ Second, clarifying that there is neither two nor three: First, pointing to the three karmas to establish non-duality.
Since even the body is no-body, speech is likewise not-speech; body and mouth are equal, and so too is the wheel of the mind.
The *Wenxin* states: "The previous passage 'should be' likely means that the Dharma-body has already been integrated; the provisional has all become real.
This merely indicates that what was taught has been integrated, but it does not yet manifest that the teacher is without distinction. Now [the author] says this is not so.

One should know that in the preceding passage, "should be" refers to the Dharma-body because the Dharma-body is preserved; "the provisional is the real" is because the real teaching is preserved. It has not yet been seen that body and speech are non-dual.
When [the distinction between] the true and the responsive bodies is obliterated, they again constitute two aspects of the three karmas;

now, when referring comprehensively to the true and responsive bodies as being "no-body," and comprehensively to the two teachings as being "no-teaching," since both body and speech are obliterated, they are equal to the mental wheel.

Therefore, the three karmas only then become non-dual. One might object that since the preceding passage identified the responsive body with the Dharma-body, it already encompasses the non-duality of the three karmas.

The single character "to speak" (shuo) refers to that which manifests the capacity by means of the object; it does not mean that what was previously spoken is the object and what is now being spoken is the capacity. Question:

Since the two—opening up the provisional and manifesting the real—are non-dual, and since the Response-body (Nirmāṇakāya) is pointed out as being identical to the Dharma-body (Dharmakāya), is this not non-duality?
Answer: Although they are non-dual, this is not the non-duality of the three karmas (body, speech, and mind) within the present text. Rather, it concerns the body and speech individually.

To say that "non-duality" refers to the finger is to mean that the finger is the Dharma-body, which is non-duality; to say it refers to the provisional is to mean it is the real, which is non-duality.
How could this mean that the body is identical to the mouth, the mouth is identical to the body, and that body and mouth are identical to the mind in their non-duality?
△ Second, establishing the transformative function through non-duality, in two parts: first, the demonstration.
Form and mind are of one suchness;
they are non-dual.
They transform without deliberation.

That which is immediately extinguished yet illuminates constitutes transformative function (*huà-yòng*). Thus, taking the principle of the non-duality of the three karmas as the basis, one manifests the transformations of body, speech, and mind, each in two modes. △ Second, the explanation:
"Constantly merging with the ultimate, one acts in accordance with things."
Regarding "Transformation": what is meant by "not deliberating, yet spontaneously reaching the ultimate through constancy"? △ Third, the summary of the non-duality of the three thousand realms:

First, it is concluded that the hundred realms are one mind and thus non-dual; Second, by using the realms as an analogy for karma, all are shown to be a single thought-moment—how could they be different?
Is it not the case that within the single mind there are the hundred realms, and within each realm there are no activities other than the three karmas?

Since the principle of non-duality lies in the fact that the three thousand [realms] are identical to a single thought-moment, the hundred realms abide within the one mind without being two, and the three karmas likewise mutually identify with one another without distinction. Why is this? Because within each and every realm, these three karmas are present.
Therefore, once again, he explains karma by means of the analogy of the realms (*dhātu*), saying:
"If even a single moment of a realm contains the three types of karma, how could they be distinct?

Since karma does not transcend the realm, and the realm itself is identical to the mind, how could karma be distinct from its nature? △ Second, showing that the fruit arises from the cause, in two parts.
First, the cause and effect are explained in general.

The functioning of the fruit is without deficiency for two reasons: first, because within each of the hundred realms, every realm possesses the three types of karma; second, because within each of the hundred realms...
The three karmas correspond to the capacities of sentient beings and thus suffer no deficiency.
The cause must accord with the fruit;
that which is realized as the fruit is such because the causal mind inherently possesses the wondrous three karmas of the hundred realms.
Application.
If one has faith, one will then know that the three mysteries have a source.

If one has faith in the completeness of the cause, one will then know that the function of the fruit consists of the three mysteries having a source. The *Bendōwa* states: "If one has faith... or, alternatively, [as follows].

Although the meaning of the two characters "no cause" (wú yīn guǒ) is not deficient, the phrasing seems incomplete; now, with four characters forming a single phrase, why should the phrasing be considered incomplete?
△ Second, specifically clarifying the merit of the fruit, in two parts: first, showing the dharma-principle of the fruit's merit.
The three karmas of the hundred realms are all empty, provisional, and middle.
"Empty, provisional, and middle" refers to the principle of the Dharma of the fruition-virtue. △ Second, showing the transformative function of the fruition-virtue:
thus, responding appropriately and universally reaching [all beings] constitutes the fruition; each manifested form and each spoken sound does not fail to encompass the hundred realms.
Is this not what is meant by the statement that "the three karmas are fully perfected, and transformations further produce transformations"?
Since the three virtues are manifested, the function of transformation is inconceivable. To respond appropriately means that the mind-wheel reaches everywhere;
thus, each individual body and speech responds to every form, manifesting the bodies that reach everywhere, and each individual voice and sound manifests the speech that reaches everywhere.
Question: How do we know that "universally responding" refers to the wheels of body and speech rather than the wheel of mind? Answer: The subsequent text states:
"As with the aforementioned wheel of mind, through its sovereign power, it causes the body and speech to respond to the capacities of both provisional and ultimate [teachings].

Taking the body of one realm as the subject that possesses and the bodies of a hundred realms as the objects possessed, the same applies to speech and mind. Furthermore, taking the body of one realm as the subject that possesses..."
The body, speech, and mind of a single realm constitute the "possessors," while the three karmas of the hundred realms are the "possessed"—the same applies to speech and mind.
Furthermore, within the body of a single realm, a single form is the "possessor" and the three karmas of the hundred realms are the "possessed";

within the speech of a single realm, a single sound is the "possessor" and the three karmas of the hundred realms are the "possessed"—the same applies to the mind as well. Within the body of a single realm, a single form-appearance manifests; this...
This transformation further manifests a hundred realms upon this form, creating yet another transformation; the same applies to speech and mind.

Because these transformations create further transformations and speech issues forth from the *Dharmasaṃgraha*, it is so called. △ Second, clarifying that the mind and the Buddha are without difference.
2. First, the formal clarification. 2.1. First, being endowed with Buddhahood from birth.
Therefore, even a single thought of an ordinary mind already possesses the principle of nature (*ri-sei*).
In terms of the Dharma, this ordinary mind is the locus where the merit is attributed; this is its capacity for universal endowment (*nōgu*).
It is the ocean of the three mysteries’ marks.
This "that which is possessed" clarifies that the Buddha’s three mysteries are possessed by sentient beings. △ Second, the Buddha possesses sentient beings.
The physical form of the retribution of a single speck of dust—that is, the physical forms of the body and speech of ordinary beings themselves—is what is possessed.
They equally abide within the fundamental principle of Vairocana.
Because Vairocana is that which all Buddhas realize as their fundamental principle, it is named the "fundamental principle" (honri), and thus it is capable of being fully possessed.
Since this principle is already possessed, it is said that they "equally abide" therein; one should know that in the preceding passage, the self was treated as the possessor. However—
In the passage following "Arising in the mind," it is stated that one's own self is the possessor (*ādhāra*), while only body and speech are cited as the possessed (*ādheya*).

When the relationship between the possessor and the possessed is manifested, then one's own three karmas (*trikarma*) are both the possessors and the possessed. When the Buddhas are the possessors, only the principle-body (*tattva-kāya*) is cited;

when the Buddhas are the possessed, only the three mysteries (*trimandala*) are cited. Because the relationship between the possessor and the possessed is thus manifested, the three [mysteries] of the principle-body [are established].

Question: Both the secret [body] and the [body of] union are the possessors (*śaktimat*), while both are the possessed (*śakti*). Regarding the principle of their essence (*tattva*), how can it be the possessed? Answer:
Because the essence is concealed by its attributes (*lakṣaṇa*), its existence is what is called "possessed. Question: The *Monshin* states that the three secrets are the functions of Vairocana.
If that is so, why is this different from the previous passage which spoke only of the possessed? Answer: This is because one does not understand the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
These two characters refer to the essence (*tattva*), which belongs to the category of the "possessor" (*dhāraka*);

one recognizes that the rational nature (*rig-pa'i rang-bzhin*) is identical to the three secrets (*triguhyasamaya*), while all their functions are the "possessed" (*dheya*). Question: Why is it said they are "together"? Answer:

It is said that "a single atom" (*eka-rajas*) is cited as an example because it exists together with all phenomena within the body of the Tathāgata Vairocana. The meaning is that this essence likewise [exists] among all phenomena.
Because not a single atom of the Dharma is excluded, it is said that they "together abide" therein;
furthermore, it is not only the ordinary mind that exists within this essence, but even a single atom likewise abides within it.

Moreover, it is not only the function of the Tathāgata’s three mysteries that exists within this essence, but even the ordinary dust likewise resides therein. Question: Why is it called the "Ocean of Marks"? Answer: Regarding the ocean—its...

The merit of a single word resides in principle (*li*), while its application lies in phenomena (*shi*). Regarding the fact that phenomena are boundless: if one asks whether the ordinary mind possesses these characteristics, the answer is as follows.
Those who follow the school of Pure Enlightenment (*Jingjue*) take the nature of conventional usage as that which is "possessed" (*suoju*) and emptiness as that which "possesses" (*nengju*);
therefore, they say it "possesses nature. Now, however, we see that emptiness is not the conventional nature; this is the position of the Four Ming [School].
Since the three mysteries possessed by this [Tathāgata] have both essence (*svabhāva*) and form (*lakṣaṇa*), they universally encompass both essence and form. Now, we ask:

are these three mysteries the ultimate nature (*dharmatā*), or are they the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), or are they emptiness (*śūnyatā*)? If one says they are conventional, then even within emptiness they are seen not to be the conventional nature.
If one says they are emptiness, then they would not be the three mysteries. Therefore, what is now being correctly explained is the very substance of the single character "nature" (*svabhāva*).

This emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is that which is capable of being endowed with; it is precisely because it is capable of being endowed with the nature of the three mysteries (*triguhyaka*) that one perceives emptiness as being identical to the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
If someone were to ask, "Is it endowed with nature (*svabhāva*) or is it endowed with characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*)?

one should answer: "From the perspective of that which is capable of being endowed, it is called 'endowed with nature'; from the perspective of that which is endowed, it is called 'endowed with characteristics. This is detailed as in the *Zong* (The School).

Wen Yuan asked: "Regarding the ocean-like characteristics of the three mysteries, what is the meaning of calling them 'characteristics'? He replied: "They are specifically associated with body and speech; generally, all three are 'characteristics.
By this principle, the mystery of mind can be compared to and distinguished from body and speech. △ Second, the conclusion and demonstration.
Only then can it be called the "three non-differentiations.

Although there are distinctions between the mind, the Buddha, and the three [realms] regarding delusion and enlightenment or high and low, the three karmas are non-dual; thus they are one essence without distinction.
Not only is the wondrous Buddha the mind that gives rise [to it], but the mind that gives rise [to it] is also the wondrous Buddha. △ Third, the conclusion.
This is established through the gate of the non-duality of self and others;
since the self is precisely the benefiting of others, the three karmas are manifested. △ First, the heading.
Regarding the ninth, the gate of the non-duality of the provisional and the real:
This gate takes the Middle Way of a single nature as the essence of non-duality. Regarding the provisional and the real, the *Miaojiji* states:

"One should know that the four teachings—whether eighty, one hundred and twenty, or one hundred and sixty [teachings]—when taken together, constitute this inconceivable unity of the provisional and the real.
This means that within the essence of the body [of reality], there is the provisional which corresponds to the real; were it not so, it would not be [the truth]."
The *Lotus Sūtra* is likewise thus: those who do not know that these provisional and real [teachings] are themselves the essence become Buddhas outside the essence;
those who know them are within the essence. Since the dharma-body does not depart from the ninefold and the one, the provisional and real teachings are now explained:

the teaching of the perfect reality (*pariniṣpanna*) is provided for the capacities of the Buddha-realm, while the teaching of the partial provisionality is provided for the capacities of the nine realms, as follows.

The text states that there are nine provisional [teachings] and one real [teaching]. This current passage establishes this distinction based on the teachings themselves, rather than the recipients of those teachings;
the latter refers to the two kinds of wondrousness regarding the benefits for the retinues who receive the moisture of the Dharma.

However, the names, meanings, and essential bodies of these provisional and real paths are difficult to distinguish. I shall now briefly indicate them, taking the ten realms and the ten suchnesses as the basis.

Regarding the clarification of the provisional and the real: if one takes such emptiness as the real, then the mutual retributions and causes and effects of the ten realms are all conventional and thus termed provisional (the meaning of essence and function).
If one takes such [emptiness] as the Middle and the real, then the mutual retributions, emptiness, and the provisional are all provisional (the meaning of the Middle and the extremes).
If one takes such [emptiness] as belonging solely to the reality of the single nature of equality—ten...
The characteristics, retributions, and emptiness of the ten realms—these three are all termed provisional (the meaning of "wanzhao").
If one takes these [three] as the reality of the Three Truths, then the characteristics and retributions of the ten realms are all dharmas produced by causes and conditions;

being encompassed within the Three Paths, they are all termed provisional (the meaning of "guode"). Regarding the attribution of these [provisional phenomena] to the Three Truths, according to the *Miaojiji*, the four types of noble beings are...
Matters proceed from cause to fruit; the six paths of existence are likewise both matters and [the locus of] correspondence.

Since cause and fruit are identical, how could the ten meanings be lacking? The text takes the ten meanings of cause and fruit as "matters" because each of the ten realms possesses its own cause and fruit.
As the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) states: "To say that the ten realms do not encompass all matters is precisely to refer to the characteristics, nature, and retribution of the ten realms."

Since it is stated that "taking equal cause and effect as the matter" refers to phenomena (xiang), nature (xing), and retribution (bao) as the matter, how can one say that the principle encompassed by the Three Truths is not exhaustive?

It should be understood that these very elements constitute the Three Truths. Furthermore, the reason the Buddha-realm can be considered the three paths arising from conditions is analogous to the fact that although practices for the sake of phenomena and provisional truth may give rise to pure karma, they are still subsumed within the realm of defilement; thus, the teachings and practices are [so categorized].

Although conditions arise from the Buddha-realm, how can this purity be turned back into delusion as if it were real? To discern [reality] through delusion is entirely subsumed within the three paths.

If one does not discuss the natural, inherent virtue of the Three Truths apart from the phenomena of turning back from delusion and arising through conditions, then the Three Truths belong to the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
The various meanings above are discussed solely in relation to the two designations of the provisional and the real.

If one establishes "neither provisional nor real" as the counter-position to that which is both provisional and real, then within the aforementioned essence, the provisional aspect of the four meanings of the "perishing virtues" is absent;
thus, they are all designated as "neither provisional nor real. The provisional aspects of the ten realms and ten suchnesses are all termed "provisional," yet they are also "real";
this should be understood as taking the ten suchnesses of the Buddha-realm as the "real," while the ten suchnesses of the nine realms are [the provisional].

Since the provisional [truth]—in terms of the dependent origination of faults and virtues and the conventional matters of essence and function—all possess the ten realms, they are encompassed by both the provisional and the real.
If one distinguishes between the two extremes of the Middle and the Extremes (*madhyānta*) by way of the realms and suchness (*tathatā*):

the six destinies are "provisional" (*prajñapti*), the two vehicles and the Buddha are "empty" (*śūnya*), and Bodhisattvas pervade both the empty and the provisional; furthermore, the Buddha is taken as...

The nine realms are empty because they are provisional; thus, while emptiness is real, the provisional is a skillful means. If one considers both illumination and non-illumination together, or distinguishes them according to the *dharmadhātu-tathatā* (the suchness of the realms), one may take the Buddha and Bodhisattvas as encompassing all three truths, while the remaining eight realms reside within emptiness and the provisional.

Alternatively, one may distinguish them such that the Buddha is the Middle Truth as the Real, while the nine realms are Emptiness and the Provisional. However, in the present text, the focus lies precisely on the "both-and" perspective.
The phrase "neither of the two" encompasses two meanings: first, the Middle and the Extremes; second, Non-extinction and Illumination.

Being neither provisional nor real constitutes Non-extinction and the Middle, while being both provisional and real constitutes the Extremes and Illumination. Therefore, the profound synthesis of the five distinctions is termed "provisional and real.
The preceding four are provisional dharmas, while the final one is the real dharma; yet, upon detailed analysis, each possesses its own aspects of the provisional and the real.
Furthermore, based on these two meanings, this inconceivable provisional and ultimate is the domain of the two wisdoms of all Buddhas of the three periods.
Since the Buddha’s two wisdoms take the conventional as the provisional and the Middle Way as the ultimate, the *Wenju* states: "The Wisdom of All Modes is called the ultimate;
the Wisdom of the Path is called the provisional. It does not mention emptiness because it is either subsumed within or returns to the Middle Way.

Alternatively, they may be unified and returned to the mundane; since what is illuminated by these provisional and real [truths] already encompasses the realm of the three truths, that which is neither provisional nor real is precisely the single nature (*ekasvabhāva*).
Regarding the "phrases within the medicinal herbs," if analyzed through the ten realms (*daśadhātu*), there is both difference and non-difference:

the Record states that because they are empty, there is difference yet no difference; because they are provisional, there is no difference yet there is difference; and because they are the middle, they are neither.

Since there is neither difference nor non-difference—taking the Buddha-realm as the reality of non-difference which belongs to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and the nine realms as the provisional of difference which belongs to the conventional (*saṃvṛti*)—one knows that the Middle Way is not merely "both. Therefore, the present text must encompass both meanings:
the Middle and the extremes, and cessation and illumination. [The author] asks: Why do all the masters take only the nine realms and the one [Buddha-realm] upon the level of conventional truth?

Regarding the distinction between the provisional and the real, why is it that they are not currently employed? The answer is: within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), taking the Buddha as the "real" encompasses two meanings.
First, for example, according to the conventional truth, if one looks toward emptiness (*śūnyatā*), he is designated as a "phenomenon" (*vastu*);

yet, if discussing the conventional itself, it also encompasses both phenomena and principle (*li*). Therefore, the *Fuxingji* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning) takes the *saṃsāra*-like samādhis as "principle" and supernatural powers and transformations as "phenomena."

Phenomena constitute "matters. When the ten realms of existence are viewed in relation to the principle within emptiness, they are real; therefore, the ten realms are matters and are provisional (*upāya*).
However, when discussing the provisional and the real from the perspective of the matters themselves, the nine realms are provisional and the Buddha-realm is real.
Furthermore, among the ten realms, the Buddha-realm—which arises through conditions (*pratītyasamutpanna*)—is able to manifest the Middle Way; therefore, it is called "real" and is ultimately real.
These characters ultimately return to the central principle, or to emptiness, or to the Three Truths;

as for the mere conventional, it can only be described as the provisional of tenfold distinctions. Now, I simply ask: regarding the matters of the conventional truth, are they distinct or non-distinct?
If one says they are non-distinct, the *Myōki* states that "the identity with the provisional is precisely distinction. If one says they are distinct, then distinction is precisely [non-distinction].
Because provisional and ultimate are fundamentally without distinction, the *Myōku* (Wondrous Verse) states: "Through wisdom and skillful means, there are provisional distinctions;
yet when all reach the ground of wisdom, there are no distinctions. Therefore, the essence of non-duality in this gate is either the single nature (*ekadhātu*) or the Middle Way.
**II. Explanation of the Two [Truths]** **A. Clarifying Provisional and Ultimate** **1. The Whole Body as Illumination and Function**
The Great Wisdom of Equality constantly mirrors the Dharma-realm.
Its entire body of equality illuminates the function of the Dharma-realm; this "Great Equality" admits of two interpretations.

First, "equality" refers to the principle of the Middle Way, while "great" invokes the functions of emptiness and conventionality, or the provisional and the real. Thus, the phrase explains the "Treasure" within the Sūtra.
Regarding "equal great wisdom" (*samata-mahāprajñā*): this is the wisdom of all Buddhas, analogous to the principle of walking with even steps as mentioned previously.

There are two kinds of equality: first, the equality of phenomena (*dharma-samatā*), which is the principle of the Middle Way; second, the equality of sentient beings (*sattva-samatā*), wherein all sentient beings equally attain the Buddha-wisdom.
"Great" (*mahat*) carries the same meaning of loftiness and vastness as explained previously. In terms of contemplating the mind, it refers to the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).
The vertical and so forth are the provisional contemplation (*parikalpita*), while the horizontal and so forth are the middle-way contemplation (*paratantra*).

When the horizontal and vertical are equally and simultaneously illuminated in their state of equality, this is precisely the Great Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-mahājñāna*). The *Wenji* states: "There are two aspects of equality:

'equality of phenomena' refers to the principle (*tattva*) contemplated by the Great Wisdom; 'attaining it together' means that all employ the causal principle to reach the fruition. If the principle being contemplated and [the principle of] the multitude...
The arising of difference is not called "Great Wisdom" (*mahāmati*). As the text says, "Dharmas are equal," which is the principle of the Middle Way;

thus, one knows that equality is the Middle Way. Since it is called "Great," as previously stated regarding its height and breadth, one should know that this height and breadth must encompass two meanings:
first, the Middle Way itself possesses the virtue of height and breadth, and the essence of this virtue of height and breadth is the Middle Way itself.
This takes emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as "high" and the provisional (*prajñapti*) as "broad"; now, because we follow this sequential meaning, they are assigned to emptiness and the provisional.

Furthermore, it is said that "equally illuminating both" is precisely the Great Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-mahājñāna*). This means that from the essence of the Middle Way, the function of dual illumination arises; therefore, it is called the Great Wisdom of Equality.
It illuminates its own essence for self-cultivation and illuminates the capacities [of beings] to transform others. Furthermore, it is said to be "constant."
To discern and grasp the meaning of "illuminating according to capacity" (*jianqu zhaoji*) is to take the essence as function;

that is, using emptiness and the provisional to illuminate the capacities for the provisional and the real across the ten dharma-realms. These two are equal and should penetrate the three truths (*sandi*).

In the practice of contemplating the mind (*guanxin*), these three truths constitute the principle of equality that is illuminated, while wisdom (*hui*) is that which performs the illumination; therefore, wisdom is called "great," and this greatness further encompasses the three [truths].
Thus, by means of the three types of wisdom, one illuminates the substance of the three truths within one’s own practice, wherein the entire substance functions as its activity;

and one illuminates the ten realms through the three provisional and real aspects of emptiness, provisionality, and the middle, according to the capacities of beings. If one relies on this meaning, the three within the substance are, in their very place, one;
they are neither provisional nor real. Yet, when illuminating the ten realms, they manifest as provisional and real; within the Buddha-realm, the ninth realm is real.

The realms (*dhātu*) are conventional, while emptiness and the two directions [of the Middle Way] together constitute the perfection of "forgetting" and "illumination. Furthermore, the passage on "contemplating the mind" also concerns the Middle and the Extremes;
emptiness is equal only in the vertical sense, while the provisional is equal only in the horizontal sense. Therefore, these two sides are not called "equality. Question:
The correct principle states that this is from the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*; why then do you now take the "wondrous phrases" to explain it? Answer: This is because one must contemplate the intent of Jingxi.

The *Myōku-ki* (Record of the Wondrous Verses) explains the verse, stating: "It is the principle (*li*) contemplated by Mahāmati," and further, "All employ the principle of the cause to reach the fruit, etc.

This is similar in meaning to the current text, which says: "Also, by virtue of the rational nature (*li-xing*), through nine provisional [teachings] and one real [teaching], one reaches the fruit by acceding to the single fundamental principle.
These words may be used to explain the phrase "constantly contemplating" (*chang-jian*), as its substance (*ti*) is this very principle.

Because it does not depart from its functioning, it is said to "constantly mirror the dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*); this refers to the dharma-realm of the three truths: emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. Question:

Why is the constant mirroring of the dharma-realm restricted solely to the provisional and the real? Answer: Because we are now taking up the illumination of sentient beings according to their capacities for the provisional and the real;
therefore, below it is simply stated that there are nine provisional [aspects] and one real [aspect], yet these provisional and real entities are eternally equal.
Because it is neither provisional nor ultimate, there is a subsequent statement that "the characteristics [of phenomena] are darkly merged with the single thought-moment and cannot be distinguished.
△ Second, the correspondence with the fruit as inherent principle is divided into two parts; first, the inherent principle.
This also arises from the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
"Capable of being endowed with" may refer to the Middle Way or to the One Nature.
While there are nine provisional aspects and one real aspect, that which is endowed— the ten realms— is both provisional and real.
