In reality, there are nine realms.
Regarding the term "furthermore" (*fù*), it means returning, reverting, or restoring; however, I now say this is not so—it means "repeatedly.
This is because the Buddha-realm repeatedly contains the nine realms, as it is said that they manifest in mutual layers.
The provisional [teachings] are likewise so.
This single character "fù" (also/again) should be interpreted in two ways: first, as above, it signifies that the provisional [teachings] of the nine realms are also repeatedly possessed of Buddhas;
second, because the nine [realms] are treated as examples of the Buddha, it says "likewise again," meaning that the nine provisional [teachings] are repeatedly possessed of [Buddhas].
The Buddha-realm is likewise; as the Buddha further possesses nine realms, the provisional and the real are mutually merged within the hundred realms in a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*).

When these realms are merged in a single thought-moment, this is the nature that is neither provisional nor real. Since the provisional and the real are one, the nature and its characteristics are mutually merged.
Because there are one hundred realms, they are subsumed and returned to a single thought-moment;
they are beyond conceptual differentiation and are spontaneously and eternally so.
If the first phrase is read in conjunction with what precedes it, it is because the hundred realms exist within a single thought-moment, and thus cannot be divided.

The subsequent phrases may be read individually to connect with the preceding meaning: the hundred realms, whether provisional or real, both affirmed and negated, are all present within the principle of nature (li-xing), spontaneously and eternally so.
This may also be understood according to the explanations of various masters. Question: Is the principle of the hundred realms characterized by marks (xiang) or markless (wuxiang)?
Answer: It is not permitted to definitively establish it as either marked or markless; rather, one should harmonize them as "eternal marks" and "eternally markless. Thus it is.
"Realization" (*liao*) means to vaguely discern the [inherent] equipment. △ Second, "the fruition accords with reality" (*guo qi*).
Upon reaching fruition, one accords with the fundamental principle of oneness; it is neither provisional nor real, yet it is both provisional and real.
The essence of the rational nature (*li xing*) is neither cause nor fruit, yet it is both cause and fruit. Because one now realizes it as the fruit, it is called "reaching" (*zhi*).
The fruit is precisely the knowledge that the principle of the preceding cause resides within it; this single principle is none other than the single nature of equality (*samatā-eka-svabhāva*).
This single nature is neither the reality of the Middle Way within the Buddha-realm, nor is it the provisional [expedients] of emptiness and the conventional within the nine realms.
Therefore, this single nature is said to be "neither provisional nor real," yet it is simultaneously able to illumine the reality of the Middle Way within the Buddha-realm and the nine realms.
Because the realms are the provisional [aspect] of emptiness, this single nature can manifest both the provisional and the real;
based on the meanings of "forgetting" and "illumination," it is explained in this way. Furthermore, this principle is precisely the Middle Way.

This Middle Way is neither the reality of the true emptiness of the Buddha-realm, nor the provisionality of the conventional existence of the nine realms, yet it is simultaneously able to illumine the true emptiness of the Buddha-realm.
The reality of this [Middle Way] is the provisional skillful means of the nine realms' conventional existence; thus, within this Middle Way, one can exercise both the provisional and the real.

Based on the meaning of "middle" and "extremes," it is explained in this manner. Furthermore, the middle and extremes may also be termed "non-extinction" and "illumination. This is because the Middle Way is capable of both non-extinction and illumination.

Now, in order to establish names that clarify and distinguish the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), we discuss them by pairing them as three and one, taking "non-extinction" as the primary term.

Regarding the "Illumination of the Two" (*Zhao er yi*), it should be understood that this treatise serves as a commentary on both the *Madhyāntavibhāga* (Distinguishing the Middle from the Extremes) and the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha* (Compendium of the Mahāyāna). Now, a question is raised:

"What is the difference between the 'adhering to the fundamental single principle' mentioned here and the 'original nature is one' mentioned previously? The answer is: If we consider them in terms of the negation of illumination (*wang zhao*), their meaning is identical.

However, if we consider them in terms of the two locations—the Middle and the Extremes—there is a difference. Previously, emptiness (*śūnyatā*) was taken as the single nature; now, [the focus is on]...
The Middle Way constitutes a single nature. If the preceding text were to take emptiness and non-existence as this single nature, one could not say that it is neither self nor other;
for the principles of these various dharma-gates each follow their own course, and their intended meaning is profound and subtle, not to be grasped hastily.

△ Second, the reconciliation of the three karmas. Part one: Showing that the three karmas all encompass both the provisional and the real. Now, within this text, the reconciliation of the three karmas is for two reasons:
first, because the provisional and real teachings explained therein belong to the wheel of speech (*vākkarma*), and speech must be manifested through the body;
furthermore, these body and speech must first be reflected upon by the mind. Thus, they are reconciled. Second, because the provisional and real universally pervade the three [karmas].

The preceding section clarified that the distinction between the provisional and the real resides specifically in the wheel of speech; therefore, it must now be interpreted and reconciled. Furthermore, there are two parts: first, the demonstration.
This means that, as previously explained regarding the mastery of the mind-wheel, it causes the body and speech to respond to the capacities of beings according to the provisional and the real.
If it were not for the mind-wheel discerning the capacities for the provisional and the real, how could the body and speech initiate responses through the provisional and the real?

The response-body accords with provisional capacities and the true-body accords with real capacities; the same applies to the mouth. Thus, one knows that the three karmas all penetrate both the provisional and the real.
△ Second, the conclusion, in two parts: first, concluding that the three karmas all penetrate both the provisional and the real.
The three karmas and a single thought-moment do not conflict with the provisional and the real.
Since the three karmas are thus identical in essence to a single thought-moment, their provisional and real aspects pervade all three karmas, universally possessing the absence of a vehicle.
△ Second, regarding the three karmas, the conclusion reveals that the provisional and the real are non-dual yet dual.
How could giving while remaining unmoving involve any separation or distinction?

One phrase corresponds to the three karmas mentioned above, and one phrase corresponds to the provisional and the real; thus, the three karmas are used to conclude and manifest the provisional and the real.
The first phrase indicates that while the single nature remains unmoving, the three karmas are manifested—this is the principle functioning as phenomena. This is the intended analogy.

The concluding summary clarifies that one should know that the provisional and the real are neither provisional nor real, yet they constitute the provisional and the real, and thus they constitute the provisional and the real.
How could they be separated? They are not separated because phenomena and principle do not separate from one another; therefore, it is possible for principle to be phenomena.
If they were separated, it would be impossible for that which is neither provisional nor real to function as the provisional and the real.
Therefore, the intent of this passage is to clarify that while the non-dual is manifested as dual, it has not yet been pointed out that the dual is non-dual.
Generally speaking, since the three karmas are thus, if they are applied as provisional or ultimate while being identical to their nature, how could they differ from that nature?

Furthermore, since the provisional and the ultimate are applied without moving from the three karmas, how could there be any separation or difference when responding to the capacities of sentient beings? This is because [the response] follows accordingly.

They come by means of the provisional and the real according to capacity; this does not mean that the provisional and the real of this gate are without distinction from the three karmas of the previous gate.
△ Second, showing that the provisional and the real are specifically located in the wheel of speech, in two parts: first, showing their distinct characteristics.
Regarding speech, it is designated by means of the provisional and the real; regarding the person, it is named by means of the true and the responsive.
If one asks: "If the three karmas each encompass both the provisional and the real, why did the preceding text specifically designate the provisional and the real as the Wheel of Speech?
To address this, the text now clarifies: △ Second, the conclusion on non-duality.
The principle of the three karmas is identical in that the provisional and the real are darkly unified.
This general statement reveals the particular; furthermore, by citing the capacity [of the teaching], it reveals the reason why the three karmas can be so:
since they are of one single nature and non-dual, the provisional and the real as taught are likewise darkly unified, without any discrepancy. If one attains this now...
The commentary does not repeat itself redundantly because the preceding text still treated non-duality as duality, whereas the present text clarifies duality as non-duality.
△ Third, the conclusion: This is established through the gate of the non-duality of the three karmas.
Because the three karmas are capable of acting as the agent that brings about what is to be accomplished, this section exists. △ First, the heading:

Regarding the "Gate of the Ten Receptions of Moistening Being Non-dual," this gate takes the Middle Way of single nature as the essence of non-duality. As for "receiving moistening," it refers to the four retinues.
Because they obtain ten benefits, they are called "those who receive moisture. Regarding the classification according to the text and phrases, there are six sections;
the fifth is "receiving moisture," which establishes the present title. One should know that receiving moisture has both general and specific aspects.

Specifically, it refers only to the three types of grasses and two types of trees, which grow through being moistened. Generally speaking, even the earth can receive moisture; however, here we follow the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

A single rain moistens the provisional [teachings] of the three types of grasses and two types of trees, as well as the real [teaching] of the single earth; therefore, it is called "receiving moisture.
If one discusses the fact that they receive the moisture of a single rain, the two characters for "receiving moisture" themselves constitute non-duality.

However, because the moisture-received objects—the grasses, trees, earth, the provisional, and the real—are distinct, they belong to duality; yet, insofar as they are all moistened by the same single rain, they are identical.
The name "non-dual" (advaya) is itself that which moistens; that which is moistened is dual. Furthermore, because it functions as the manifestor of what is manifested, the rain is also dual.
As the *Myōki* states: "Now, we derive these distinct names from what is rained down. If this is so, how does this differ from grasses and trees? The answer is:
grasses and trees receive their names solely from the grasses and trees themselves, whereas clouds and rain receive their names from what they manifest.
Therefore, they are not the same. If one distinguishes them based on the ground that serves as the locus for the intercalation, there are two types:
grasses and trees. Both grow from the same ground; this is the reality (*tattva*) of non-differentiation. Yet, the grasses and trees themselves represent the provisional (*upāya*) differentiation.

Because the provisional differs from the real, they are "two"; because the real accords with the provisional, they are "not-two. This essence of non-duality is either emptiness (*śūnyatā*) or the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).
Now, if one does not rely on this [distinction] to explain non-duality, the text itself relies on the fact that the earth and grasses are both composed of the same four subtle elements (*catur-aṇu*);
therefore, they are non-dual. Thus, these four subtle elements serve as a universal metaphor for both the single nature and the Middle Way.
Being neither provisional nor real, they constitute the essence of non-duality; hence, one must explain the provisional and the real in relation to those who accept the intercalary month.
Knowing this, one correctly grasps the profound text’s discourse on awakening through principle to unravel the various provisional and real [teachings] as being identical;

thus, even provisional and real cannot be apprehended as dual, and are therefore non-dual. Furthermore, knowing that in the Perfect Teaching, the opening [of the teaching] is discussed according to stages, and that when measured by these stages, there is still the benefit of the three grasses and two woods;
yet, when one investigates their ultimate destination, the Perfect is but a single ground. If, by means of...

Now, facing the gate, one selects between the self and the other; although the gate also encompasses the capacity (the *ki*), it uses the response to that capacity to demonstrate non-duality, rather than discussing non-duality from the perspective of the capacity itself.
Regarding the provisional and the real, the three karmas are all discussed as non-dual from the standpoint of the responsive capacity.
△ Second, the explanation has two parts: first, receiving the Dharma-principle; second, the initial indication.
The fundamental nature of phenomena inherently possesses both the provisional and the real.

Regarding "phenomena" (wu) as the objects of capacity and "principles" (li) as the principles themselves, from the very beginning there exists a nature of "double negation" (neither-one-nor-many) that acts as the possessor,
while the provisional and the real act as that which is possessed.
The熏習 (*vāsanā*) from beginningless time may be either real or provisional.

However, the meaning of *vāsanā* is explained extensively in the *Awakening of Faith*, and it is also discussed in the *Fuxing ji* (Commentary on the *Mohe Zhiguan*). Now, based on the textual intent of these two sources, I shall attempt to analyze it.
As for *vāsanā*, there is that which perfumes (*neng xun*) and that which is perfumed (*suo xun*); the inherent nature (*xingju*) of both good and evil serves as the object to be perfumed.
Furthermore, regarding the capacity for perfuming, there are two aspects: the phenomenal and the noumenal, each of which has both internal and external dimensions.

First, when discussing the phenomenal and the noumenal in contrast: taking the single nature of equality as the perfumer is internal perfuming; taking the cultivation of good and evil within practice as the perfumer is external perfuming.

Second, when discussing the internal and external from the perspective of phenomena themselves: if one examines the internal and external in terms of wholesome dharmas, generally there are... [text ends]
Regarding these four: first, in terms of wisdom and practice, taking wisdom as internal and practice as external;
second, in terms of primary and auxiliary [causes], taking the wisdom of the primary cause as internal and the wisdom of the auxiliary causes as external;

third, in terms of the supported and the support, taking the cultivation of goodness arising from the six faculties of the primary retribution as internal permeation and the cultivation of goodness arising through the six external sense objects as external permeation; fourth.

Regarding oneself, one’s own ability to cultivate goodness based on the primary and secondary conditions serves as internal perfuming (*adhyātma-vāsanā*), while relying on the power of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to cultivate goodness serves as external perfuming (*bāhya-vāsanā*). By analogy with the good, this also applies to evil.
Those who commit evil are certainly not insentient; they must possess consciousness. However, this consciousness is a mind of ignorance (*avidyā-citta*) that acts as the perfumer.
That which is called "internal" (analogous to "wisdom" within the category of the wholesome) arises from the mind conditioned by ignorance and constitutes volitional formations (*saṃskāra*);

because these formations perform evil deeds, they act as perfumers (*vāsaka*), and are thus termed "external" (analogous to "volitional formations" within the category of the wholesome). The remaining three [categories] may all be explained by analogy as being either internal or external.
One should know that the arising of both good and evil necessarily proceeds through these four acting as perfumers, whether in terms of the phenomena themselves...

In the context of the mutual correspondence between principle and phenomena, although the four meanings are all external perfuming, it is by means of the principle that True Suchness (tathatā) is capable of possessing [these qualities] that they constitute internal perfuming.
This is because its essential nature is constantly perfuming what it possesses; thus, even during the stage of the nature (xing), the meaning of perfuming already exists.

When external perfuming encounters the appropriate conditions, the nature within cultivation (xiu-zhong zhi xing) is immediately produced. Failing to perceive this intent, one merely provides an exegesis of the present [text].
Furthermore, it must be understood that the preceding thought serves as the perfumed (*bhāvyamāna*) and the succeeding thought serves as the perfumer (*bhāvaka*).
Whether internal or external, this is but a single true nature (*tattva-svabhāva*). When the mind of true nature perfumes the object of true nature, the true nature is thereby manifested.

This may also be described as the true mind perfuming the true object; through the sequence of true perfuming, the true and the true mutually perfume one another, whereby one naturally enters [enlightenment].

Regarding the "beginningless perfuming" mentioned in the current text, this refers precisely to the two types of perfuming— internal and external— within the realm of phenomena (*dharma*) acting as the perfumers,
while the inherent potential for the provisional and the real (*śakti-sampad*) acts as the perfumed. Because of that perfuming, the entire nature is realized as cultivation,
whereby the distinct benefits of both the provisional and the real are attained.
The provisional and the real are fundamentally equal by virtue of the principle of permeation (*vāsanā*).

As for the difference in their two benefits, it arises because the capacity to manifest them through cultivation is fully developed; since the provisional and the real are originally one, they are said to be equal.

Furthermore, the provisional and the real possessed by each person are inherently present within everyone, yet they differ according to individual permeation; thus, some individuals may manifest the provisional.

Alternatively, while one person may manifest the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), in truth every individual possesses both the provisional (*upāya*) and the ultimate; therefore, it is said to be "equal. △ Second, the explanation:
when meeting with the appropriate time, one forms habits, which are supported by practice and vows.

The commentary on the preceding text states: "Regarding 'beginningless perfuming'—from time immemorial, when the conditions for mutual resonance between the capacity [of the practitioner] and the response [of the Buddha] are met, then habituation is formed.

Habituation is internal perfuming; practice and vows are external perfuming. This applies to the internal and external aspects of wisdom and conduct, as well as the internal and external aspects of the primary and auxiliary [practices].
It also extends to the internal and external aspects of the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya* and *adhiṣṭhāna*). Because it traverses the external..."
Because one arouses vows and practices amidst the dust of the world, one comes to know that all practices and vows of Samantabhadra’s contemplation arise from this;
if there were no fundamental cause of permeation (*vāsanā*), these would be established in vain.

To explain the previous point regarding the original, inherent possession of the provisional and the real, it may also be said: if there were no permeation, even such inherent possession would be in vain.

Suppose that [the distinction between] the provisional and the real arises from the difference in their respective perfuming (*vāsanā*) rather than from a difference in their intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*).
To explain the above principle that the provisional and the real are eternally equal through perfuming, this section is interpreted as follows: [Exegesis].
As shown above, the meaning of this section is already clear; how could it be the same as the various masters who fear the text will become overly prolix?
Regarding the passage cited above, it merely states that "internal permeation" occurs when one encounters the proper time and practices accordingly, while "external permeation" occurs otherwise.
However, I maintain that this is not the case. The preceding text simply speaks of "beginningless permeation"; how can we know that this refers exclusively to internal permeation?
Regarding this, Master Ye’s interpretation of *yùtóng* (encountering and penetrating) as "the present day" in contrast to "beginningless time" below is not yet correct.

If one simply speaks of "encountering," how can it be determined that this refers to the present day? According to the correct principle, taking "beginningless habitual perfuming" (*wúshǐ xūnxí*) as "encountering" refers to the provisional and ultimate teachings (*quánshí jiào*).

Taking "forming habits through encountering" (*chéngxí*) and so forth as "encountering the teaching" implies the presence of both understanding (*jiě*) and practice (*xíng*). As for "forming habits," it is... [text ends]
Understanding, practice, and vows constitute "external perfuming" (wàixūn); that which is intrinsically endowed with both the provisional and the real is termed "internal perfuming" (nèixūn).
Now I ask: does that which is intrinsically endowed act as the perfumer (néngxūn) or as the perfumed (suǒxūn)? According to the correct principle, it is said:

"Therefore, one should know that if the nature’s goodness and the nature’s evil are not clarified, internal perfuming remains obscure. Thus, the *Fǔxíngchú* states: "By means of what is internally possessed..."
Therefore, according to the *Longshu* (Dragon Commentary), this [passage] takes "inherent nature" (*xingju*) as the "perfumable" (*soxun*).
If that were so, and if there were only external perfuming acting upon internal endowment, would it not follow that the internal endowment itself lacks any capacity for perfuming?

If one claims that the inherent nature of good and evil constitutes the "perfumer," I do not yet understand what is being pointed to as the "perfumable. Thus, it is known that [the interpretation] is incomplete.
The passage stating that "the True Suchness skillfully and constantly perfumes" results in the internal endowment being constantly perfumed; therefore, it is not accepted here.
△ Second, explaining the reception of the intercalary month and the response of resonance has two parts: first, showing the resonance; second, first, the general establishment.
Although their natures are without distinction,
when the former is cited to give rise to the latter,
it must necessarily depend upon the manifestation of illusion.

The capacity to initiate [the response] belongs to that which is to be responded to, while the occasion for initiation belongs to the recipient. Xuán (玄) says: "A crossbow possesses the mechanism that can be triggered;

thus, the archer triggers it. The *zhān* (籤) states: "Sentient beings are like the crossbow, past causes are like the mechanism, the Buddha is like the archer, the response is like the triggering, and the benefit is like the arrow's impact.
Although the text mentions the response, there must necessarily be something initiated by it. △ Second, explaining the characteristics, part one.
Explaining the manifestation of illusion:
illusory capacity, illusory response, illusory resonance, and illusory engagement.
Because the nature subsumes cultivation, all are like illusions; the intent is that within the very state of illusion, there is resonance and response, pointing to the reality-as-it-is (li-ji).
In responding to the capacities of sentient beings, there is nothing that is not perfectly manifest. △ Second, the explanation of "no distinction":
both the responsive capacity and the transformed being are neither provisional nor ultimate.

Because the capacity and response are like illusions, they are neither provisional nor ultimate; since phenomena are pointed out as being identical to principle, their nature is without distinction. △ Second, the clarification.
The first of the three aspects of inherent nature is now demonstrated:

because the inherent capacity is neither provisional nor real, it constitutes the responsive capacity that is both provisional and real; likewise, the Buddha’s fruition is also inherently endowed with that which is neither provisional nor real, thereby constituting the responsive manifestation that is both provisional and real.

Because sentient beings and Buddhas share the same wondrous nature, both possess the provisional and the real to constitute the response to the capacity [of beings]. △ Second, the explanation of the two [aspects]:
first, the explanation of the provisional and the real. When the capacities of beings and the response of the Buddha accord, it is called "the capacity responding to the accord."
All things take the provisional and the real as their mechanism, and they accord with the provisional and the real.
There is no partiality regarding body and land;

both sentient beings and Buddhas each possess the provisional and the real, and each possesses their own body and land. Now, this text applies to both [the provisional and the real] in two ways, yet it is ultimately one.

The essence resides in the three lower lands because it accords with the capacities of sentient beings; furthermore, these two [lands] also encompass the *dharmakāya* of the *śāntaprabhāsvara* (the Land of Tranquil Light).
There are three reasons for this: first, because partial realization exists within the *samyaktvaniyata-rāśi* (the Land of Receiving Retribution);

second, because the supreme grade of the *śāntaprabhāsvara* is manifested to suit those capacities, such that although the capacities remain in the lower lands, the Dharma is ultimately perfected; third, because of the capacities [of the beings].

Because it universally attains the benefit of wondrous enlightenment, it is illustrated by way of analogy: regarding contemplation and regarding [the nature of] benevolence, it is discussed in terms of severance; regarding stages, it is discussed as being in the stage of wondrous enlightenment.

The capacity that achieves the benefit manifests the aspect of the benefit attained; that which achieves it resides in the capacity, in the cause, while that which is achieved resides in the Buddha, in the fruit.
Since the provisional and the real of the sentient being and the Buddha are identical, it is said to be "without partiality," which does not mean that the provisional is excluded.
Because their true self-characteristics are identical, it is said that there is no partiality. △ Second, the explanation of the "double negation" (neither... nor...).

Since they are the same as the Constantly Quiescent Light and there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm, all return to the single nature; therefore, it is said they are "the same. The land is the same as the Quiescent Light, and the body is the same as the Dharma-body; there is nothing that is not identical.
The Dharma-realm of identical meaning is the Dharmakāya. △ Third, the conclusion of the two [sections]; first, the conclusion of the response and stimulus.
Therefore, one should know that the three thousand realms are co-present within the mind-ground, and are no different from the three thousand realms of the Buddha’s mind-ground.
In both instances, the "mind-ground" (cittabhūmi) is bound above to form the Buddha of Birth; this possesses both the provisional and the real.

In both instances, the "three thousand worlds" are bound above to constitute the provisional and the real in terms of the capacity for response (yǒng) and the responsive manifestation (yìng). △ Second, binding the capacities for response to show that the moisture received is non-dual.
The four subtle elements (catur-aṇu) are identical in essence;
the provisional and the real are equal in their benefits. Within the single ground of reality, even the grasses and trees of the provisional all possess these four subtle elements.

These four subtle elements serve as a direct metaphor for the principle of non-duality; because this single nature of the Middle Way possesses the four virtues, they are thus likened to the four subtle elements of the provisional.
Regarding "actual benefit" (*shiyi*) and so forth, attaining the Dharma corresponds to attaining the four virtues of the single nature;
attaining the benefit of the fruit (*guanyi*) likewise corresponds to the four virtues of the single nature. Therefore, when receiving the intercalary month, there is no duality.
If one takes the current text and restricts the analogy of the three thousand [realms] to the four subtle elements (*catur-aṇu*), how much error would that not entail! △ Third, the conclusion.
This is established by means of the gate of the non-duality of the provisional and the real.

Because the teachings of the provisional and the real are expounded, there arise sentient beings who are capable of receiving the intercalary month. △ Third, the conclusion of the two [sections]: first, concluding the ability to present [the teaching].
Therefore, through each of these ten gates, one universally enters into both matter and mind, and even into the moisture of the *śīla* (precepts), all being thus.

The ten gates serve as the means to expound the Ten Profundities (*jūmyō*) along with the sutras, which are that which is to be expounded; thus, each of these gates that serve as the means of exposition universally allows entry.
By contemplating non-duality through the gate of non-duality, one enters the principle of non-duality: the three thousand realms in a single moment of thought.

The emptiness, the provisional, and the middle are three yet one; because they are one, they are non-dual. This non-duality is itself the subject of contemplation and itself the object of contemplation.
Since subject and object are identical as one whole, this is "entry" (praveśa) itself; it does not mean entering something else.

△ Second, the conclusion of what was presented, which has two parts. First, regarding the ten profundities (daśa-māhātmya) presented according to the text, the ten profundities of the *Xuanyan wen* are explained as follows:
The "wondrous names" (*nāman*) of the sūtra that can be expounded constitute the "expounded" (*viśeṣya*), while the present text serves as the "expounder" (*viśeṣaṇa*).

Since both this expounder and the expounded are now treated as the "expounded," the ten topical gates (*daśamukha*) serve as the "expounder. Speaking according to the underlying intent, the ten wondrous aspects (*daśamithyā*) in the *Xuanyiwen* (Profound Meaning) are precisely the wondrous names of the sūtra;
since they are all collectively termed the "expounded names," it is only in the subsequent section that the specific [content] of the sūtra being expounded is presented.
Exegesis: The first section also has two parts. First, regarding the tenfold wondrous principle that is set forth, there are again two parts. First, the heading:
"Therefore, the ten wondrous aspects are of one principle from beginning to end.

Because that which can be set forth is non-dual, that which is set forth is a single principle; just as form and mind set forth the objects of perception, and so on up to the reception of the seasonal rains.

In the *Shen juanshu liyi se xin* (The Heart-Mind of the Benefits for Retinues), it says: "All phenomena are none other than the nature of mind. In the *Nei wai zhong* (Inner and Outer Middle), it says: "There is only the single true nature;

there is neither emptiness, nor the provisional, nor the middle. In the *Xiu xing zhong* (Cultivation and Nature), it says: "To realize the nature of non-cultivation is the single wondrous vehicle. In the *Yin guo zhong* (Cause and Effect), it says:

"Cause and effect are without distinction; the principle from beginning to end is one. In the *Ran jing zhong* (Defilement and Purity), it says: [...]* *Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a larger work, likely a commentary on the *Awakening of Faith*, and the final section regarding defilement and purity is incomplete.*

In the section on "Defilement and Purity within Emptiness," it says that [the dependent and the primary] vanish of themselves; in the section on "Abiding in the Middle," it says that both the dependent and the primary dwell within the one mind;

in the section on "Self and Other," it says that the fundamental is the one nature; in the section on the "Three Karmas," it says that the realms are already contained within a single thought-moment—how could the three karmas be distinct?

In the section on "The Provisional and the Real," it says that the provisional and the real are mutually merged; in the section on "The Hundred Realms Receiving the Influence of a Single Thought-moment," it says that the provisional and the real arise from...
The principle of permeation is eternally equal, for it can manifest the tenfold wonders as being entirely one. △ Second, the explanation:
Just as the object fundamentally possesses the three [wonders], this is the wonder of the object.
Because understanding arises based on principle, it is called wisdom (*jñāna*).
Wisdom is sublime;
wisdom and understanding guide conduct.
The practice is sublime.

Because the practice and its realization accord with principle, and the three factors correspond without difference, yet are conventionally established as distinct through the designation of stages of depth and shallowness to exclude confusion—
the stages are sublime.
The three factors discussed—object, wisdom, and practice—are termed the "Three Guides" (san-gui) because they explain the Dharma according to the present context.

However, these Three Guides are themselves the single true nature; therefore, the Three Guides pervade both the beginning and the end. There is no need to analyze them here in terms of the separation or union of their essential bodies (*dharmatā*).
Since the principle of separation and union is already fully contained within them, one should simply follow the meaning of the text for now.

The principle of the beginning and the end is one; yet, when it is said that "practice and realization accord with the principle," this means that both the three aspects of practice and the three aspects of realization each individually accord with the principle.
Because they accord with the principle, and because the principle is identical, one cannot differentiate between the high and low levels of their stages.
Since there is no difference, yet they are differentiated, it is said that these distinctions of stage are "provisionally established."
The three dharmas are simply the realization of those three aspects of principle.
The excellence of the three dharmas lies in the fact that their realization is not distinct from the realization of the subtle principle of the object.
This refers to the three as the causes and fruits of one's own practice.
The final five chapters discuss the arising of the functions of the three dharmas.
The five [sections] beginning with "resonance" (ganying) demonstrate how the three dharmas arise as functions;

when these three dharmas reside within oneself, they constitute the cause and fruit of one's own practice (*xing*), and when they are directed toward others, they constitute the capacity for transformation (*hua*)—the subject and object. △ Second, "Gathering the Sublime to Form Contemplation," which has two parts. First, showing the three dharmas.
It does not depart from a single thought-moment.
Since the three dharmas are established as the three thousand in a single thought-moment—namely, emptiness, the provisional, and the middle—they possess efficacy.

This establishment constitutes the fivefold subtle practices of one's own cultivation (*svayaṃ-caryā*); thus, the *Xuánwén* states: "The preceding five [practices] are the establishment of one's own cultivation. Efficacy, moreover, refers to transformation for others (*parārtha*).

Because he is wondrous in five ways, both himself and others are, in this very instant, one thought-moment. △ Second, showing that one thought-moment encompasses both the fundamental and the manifested.
If one understands this one thought-moment, the fundamental and manifested aspects of the Dharma of the Buddhas of the ten directions are not remote.
The Way of realizing that a single thought-moment is itself the manifestation [of reality] is fully complete.

Since the fundamental and迹 (traces) of the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three thousand worlds are not separate from this present thought, it is said that they are "not remote. △ Third, showing the ultimate destination established by the ten gates.
Therefore, these ten gates are restated so that they may be recognized through contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).
Since the *Xuánwén* has already explained the Ten Subtleties (*shímiao*), and now these ten gates are restated once more, it is called a "restatement.

Furthermore, since the commentary (*qiǎnwén*) has concluded its reliance on the *Xuánwén* to explain the Ten Subtleties, these ten gates are now restated to further elucidate their profound meaning; thus, it is called a "restatement."

The intent of describing the "three thousand [realms] in a single thought" lies in making the contemplative practice (*guanxing*) clear and manifest. △ Second, the conclusion of the scriptural passage thus presented:
Since the title at the beginning is already so, one can understand that the individual elements are integrated into a comprehensive pattern.
The Ten Subtleties (*daśa-sūkṣma*)—the term "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) being the name from the title itself—are categorized generally and specifically;

since their textual content accords with their essential intent in the context of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*), they may be understood as such. *Ten Gates of Non-duality: Essential Points*, Scroll II (End).

The late Master Zhizhong of Buben once expounded this text for his disciples, exhausting its depths and reaching its subtlest points; his exposition conformed to the established rules and followed the correct tracks.

Although he scrutinized the literary elegance of the various chapters and established great principles and core tenets according to what he had attained, [the text continues:]... to the ultimate point.
Regarding the debates on points of resolution and examination, there could be no avoiding discussions of similarities and differences, strengths and weaknesses;
thus, at the request of the students, I composed this commentary, which has become a work of my own school. On the day of my passing, I entrusted it to my young son. Alas!

As the ancients said, "The shadow perishes after a hundred years, but the heart endures for a thousand ages. Therefore, it must not fail to be transmitted to future generations. I have now commissioned artisans to carve it into printing blocks.
May this work vie in brilliance with the transcribed records of other schools; for the gentleman does not take sides.
Scholars of far-reaching insight from the four quarters will surely discern the truth herein. Recorded on the last day of the seventh month in the year of Renxu, Xiangxing, by the disciple Yu Xian.
